item.title: 2027 Lamborghini Temerario Spyder: 10,250 RPM With the Top Down
item.text: How do you make an already-wicked Italian supercar that revs to 10,000 RPM even better? Easy: take the roof off and give it, uh, an even higher redline. That’s what’s up with the new 2027 Lamborghini Temerario Spyder. It keeps all the savage goodness of the “regular” Temerario, but it raises the RPM limit to 10,250 and loses the top so you can hear it better. Of course, it doesn’t just lose its top. It merely hides it via a fully retractable hardtop, a first for Lambo in this category. Previously, they’ve been all soft tops. Per the automaker, the roof system utilizes 10 electric actuators to lower and raise the roof quickly and quietly, storing it vertically behind the seats, which is how Lamborghini was able to retain the see-through engine cover in the Spyder. Lamborghini With the top down, the center of gravity drops by 3 mm compared with the closed configuration, while its longitudinal position remains practically identical and the car’s distribution is unaltered. This means the roadster’s dynamics remain just as pristine as the coupe. Per Lambo, a traditional roof setup that stashes away horizontally would’ve raised the center of gravity by approximately 7 mm and shifted it 11 mm towards the rear axle. The mighty 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 with three axial-flux electric motors remains, along with its 907 horsepower, 118 of which comes from the electric bits. The eight-speed dual-clutch transmission lets it launch from 0-60 mph in 2.8 seconds thanks to its electrified all-wheel drive, and reach a top speed of 213 mph. Bonus points if you reach that speed with the roof down. Lamborghini Besides its ability to offer endless headroom, the Spyder isn’t all that different. item.title: This Toyota GR Supra's Rear Wing Looks Like Stretched Pixels, But It's Real
item.text:
This Toyota GR Supra's Rear Wing Looks Like Stretched Pixels, But It's Real
One of the most unique wings we've seen
The Toyota GR Supra might have been dropped from the lineup, but tuners are still developing new parts for the Japanese sports car with the BMW bones. Seibon Carbon and Joevil Motorsports showcased a few interesting upgrades in their latest SEMA build, including a dramatically elongated carbon fiber hatch with an integrated wing that projects well beyond the rear bumper.
Rather than a traditional rear wing that bolts onto the rear deck, Seibon molded the entire hatch and long-tail extension out of double-sided dry carbon fiber. The top end is smooth, while the underside has four strakes – most likely for structural rigidity. The replacement hatch is compatible with the factory mounting points, meaning that the modification is reversible and doesn't require any cutting.
The stretched tail gives the GR Supra unconventional proportions better suited to the drag strip. According to the company, the shape of the wing was dictated by aero simulations. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) showed that when the gurney flap is set at 7 mm (0.28 in), there is a 6% reduction in drag alongside a 6% increase in downforce compared to the stock hatch.
As seen in the aero test results shared by the company on social media, with the gurney flap removed, drag is reduced by 10%, although downforce falls by 38%.
More carbon fiber components
Besides the fancy drag wing that stole the show, this GR Supra comes fitted with an array of dry carbon fiber components. Those include the vented hood, the pronounced splitter, the sharp side skirts, the carbon door panels and the matching front fenders, a new roof panel and a more aggressive rear diffuser. Furthermore, the company introduced a dry carbon duct replacing one of the headlights with the goal of bringing more air into the engine bay.
Of course, there are plenty of modifications under the skin to justify the exterior design. The BMW-sourced turbo 3.0-liter inline-six engine has received a KLM Race Precision Next Gen 7275 turbo, bringing a significant yet undetermined increase in the output. This is supported by a CSG Spec V3 fuel system, a CSF billet intake manifold, and an upgraded cooling system.
Power is sent to the rear wheels through an Applied Torque Solutions Stage 2 ZF8HP eight-speed automatic gearbox with a billet torque converter, a carbon fiber driveshaft, and Titan Motorsports axles. As for the Z4-derived chassis, it features Riaction coilovers, R1 Concepts rotors with Spiegler brake lines and a staggered wheel setup with aftermarket alloy wheels from BBS and Belak wrapped in Mickey Thompson drag tires.
While the complete Joevil Motorsports build serves as a rolling showcase for SEMA, Seibon Carbon confirmed that the drag wing will soon be available to order.

item.title: Lego’s New Formula 1 Speed Champions Collection Includes Tiny Versions of All 22 Current F1 Drivers
item.text:
It’s been two years since Lego and Formula 1 first partnered up to translate the excitement of the grand prix grid into tiny, plastic, painful-to-step-on brick form. But while the race cars were a realistic low-polygon tribute to the life-size real things, the minifigures that accompanied them were fairly generic. Until now, that is, because the upcoming Lego Speed Champions lineup features all 11 teams on the 2026 grid and all 22 full-time drivers, rendered with realistic driving suits and customized hair.
Announced at the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix against a backdrop of several giant minifigures and a full complement of Lego-clad go-karts (now updated with neon LED light strips for the full Vegas experience), this next batch of Speed Champions sets will go on sale March 1, 2027. That makes for plenty of time to build all 11 before the first race of the season in Bahrain, although it’s also yet another thing to wait for during the off-season.
Arvid Lindblad, driver for the Visa Cash App Racing Bulls Team, made at appearance at Lego’s press announcement, and posed with both his large and small Lego likenesses. Asked about his thoughts on the result, the British driver said: “Awesome, nailed it. They got the hair perfect,” adding that, “I’ve always loved Legos, though I never imagined having my own minifigure.”
And speaking of hair, yes, the Valteri Bottas minifigure is rocking a mullet. Each plastic hairpiece was approved by the respective drivers. “When we pitched the the hairstyles to the teams and the drivers, they absolutely loved it,” said Will Thorogood, the Lego designer who led this effort. “They all thought it was as funny as we did.”
Another key part of bringing out the driver’s personality is the helmets, which are “far more detailed than any helmet we've ever done before with the with the Lego production,” according to Thorogood. Lando Norris’s helmet, for example, “has all the blob details on it” as well as a minifigure Easter egg hidden in the design. Each driver also comes with two facial expressions on opposite sides of the minfigure head; Charles Leclerc’s visage is either relaxed in sunglasses or a more serious grimace, both with the Ferrari driver’s stubbled mustache and goatee.
The cars themselves reflect the new regulations and, says Thorogood, “as you look closely, you'll see every single one is built completely differently to capture all the aero details and principles that each of the teams has employed.” These too feature several Easter eggs for Lego fans, such as suspension wishbones made from wizard wands and rear diffuser strakes made from minifigure meat cleavers.
Measuring 7.5 inches long and 2.5 inches wide, the Speed Champions sets will be priced at $29.99 when they go on sale next year. More photos and details are viewable now on the Speed Champions section of the Lego Website.

item.title: Jeremy Clarkson's Ferrari F355 GTS Just Shattered Expectations And Set An Auction Record
item.text:
Jeremy Clarkson's Ferrari F355 GTS Just Shattered Expectations And Set An Auction Record
Former Top Gear host's 1996 F355 GTS sets a live-auction world record, helped by 15,200 miles and fully documented ownership history.
Jeremy Clarkson once called his Ferrari F355 GTS "the greatest car in the world, ever." Buyers at Iconic Auctioneers' NEC Classic Motor Show sale in Birmingham seemed to agree. The 1996 car just sold for £405,000 (about $533,000), a live-auction world record for the model.
The sale closed on November 14, 2026, nearly doubling the auctioneer's pre-sale estimate. It also settled a question hanging over the car since a failed attempt to sell it the previous year.
Iconic Auctioneers had pegged the F355 GTS at £200,000 to £250,000 (about $263,000 to $329,000) going into the sale, a range that already reflected its celebrity history. That estimate proved conservative once bidding opened on the car.
Rob Hubbard, managing director and principal auctioneer at Iconic Auctioneers, pointed to the car's documented history as the draw. He said:
'For many enthusiasts, these are cars they remember watching on television or reading about in the motoring press. Jeremy's Ferrari is a particularly good example, with a history that buyers could follow right back to his original order.'
Hubbard also weighed in on the result within the wider sale:
'To achieve these results across such different cars is very pleasing. We work closely with owners to understand what they're selling and bring it to the attention of the right buyers, whether it's a significant collector car or a more modest classic.'
The gap between this sale and the car's last outing is stark. A comparable 1997 F355 GTS sold for just £120,375 (about $158,500) in August 2025. This same car failed to find a buyer at an estimate of £180,000 to £220,000 (about $237,000 to $290,000) back in July 2025. The buyer's premium on the November sale ran 12.5 percent before VAT, 15 percent inclusive.
Jeremy Clarkson's 1996 Ferrari F355 GTS
Clarkson ordered the Ferrari new through Maranello Sales and took delivery in August 1996, making him the car's first owner according to its original Warranty Card. He later gave the F355 GTS away as a Sunday Times reader prize, a detail that adds another layer to its documented ownership chain.
The car was not the only Clarkson-connected lot at the sale. Three of his former Grand Tour cars sold for a combined £160,312 (about $206,802). A 1982 Lancia Montecarlo Spider from his collection brought £69,188 (about $91,100), setting its own live-auction world record for that model.
Other consignments matched the night's momentum. A 1986 Porsche 911 Turbo SE Flachbau once owned by Sir Ron Dennis sold for £382,500 (about $504,000), a UK live-auction record. Noel Gallagher's 1978 Rolls-Royce Silver Shadow II brought £65,250 (about $86,000), also a record for the model.
Even the sale's odder entries performed. A Reliant Supervan III sold for £70,875 (about $93,300), setting a live-auction world record of its own. Across the whole event, Iconic Auctioneers reported total sales of £14.2 million (about $18.7 million), with 81 percent of cars finding new owners.
Gallery: Jeremy Clarkson's Ferrari F355 GTS
The F355 GTS that sold for £405,000 (about $533,000) carries VIN number ZFFXR42C000106175 and shows approximately 15,200 miles on its odometer, a low figure for a car built in 1996. It retains its original V8 engine and six-speed gated manual transmission.
The car wears its factory Rosso Corsa paint over a Crema leather interior, with carbon-backed sports seats fitted from new. Iconic Auctioneers' listing included Clarkson's original order correspondence alongside the Warranty Card naming him as first owner.
That paper trail separates this sale from ordinary F355 GTS transactions, where celebrity ownership rarely comes with documentation tracing back to the factory order. Low mileage, unmolested specification and a verifiable history with a recognizable first owner shaped the final price.
The result adds to a run of notable Ferrari auction outcomes this year. It now sits alongside records set by cars including the Michael Jordan-owned Ferrari 550 Maranello and a Ferrari F50 that each broke their own model records at separate sales this autumn.
Source: Iconic Auctioneers

item.title: McLaren Revives Manual in First Stick-Shift Supercar Since F1
item.text:
If anyone truly bears the responsibility of keeping the manual transmission alive, it’s companies like McLaren, Ferrari, and Porsche—manufacturers that famously spare no expense on making their vehicles as excellent as they can be, and can frankly charge whatever they like for the privilege of ownership. But when even Maranello can’t seem to find a way to link up a true manual gearbox to its V12, something is seriously wrong.
Fortunately, this year’s Monterey Car Week has brought about a row-your-own renaissance, and the latest to finally join the party is McLaren. It’s just revealed its first manual supercar since the F1 more than 30 years ago, and it’s called the McL 6GT.
It’s a strange name, mashing up McLaren’s current Formula 1 chassis nomenclature with the spirit of its old Can-Am race cars, like the M6. Technically, what you see here is a concept, but the McL 6GT is promised to enter production in 2028, with its stick and three pedals in tow.
Modern McLarens, from the MP4-12C to the Artura and even extreme examples like the Senna and W1, tend to follow some core design tenets. There’s a familiarity in their rooflines; tapered, curved noses usually incorporating the brand’s swoopy logo as a motif; and rear ends exposed for cooling and airflow. The McL 6GT doesn’t feature any of these things, however, which might make it the company’s most unique design since it relaunched its road-car operation 15 years ago. And honestly, I think it’s perfect.
There are references to the M6 GT abound, from the vertical headlights and Kamm tail to the position and shape of every duct, rendered with a simplicity that we used to see in supercars of the ’90s and 2000s but see less today. And inside, McLaren has transformed the shifter into an art piece itself, its metallic linkages attracting natural light from every angle in a sea of black and carbon fiber. They’re clearly proud of it, and they suitably want it to be the focal point in here.
At the moment, McLaren has revealed precious few details about the McL 6GT under the skin. It’s powered by a V8, as so many of the company’s products are, though we don’t know if it’s turbocharged or naturally aspirated. There’s no hybrid assistance, as you’d guess, with the company promising a “tactile, analogue, and deeply mechanical” experience, and the monocoque and body are all made of carbon fiber.
What’s more, McLaren bills this as a “new type” of supercar “beyond the core portfolio.” Based on that, it sounds like manual transmissions aren’t about to become a standard feature of the brand; that, beyond the delineation of “Sports, Super, and Ultimate” models of the past, McLaren is diversifying into more exclusive offerings that, at least in this particular case, pursue a more analog experience counter to the regular lineup. For now, anyway.
It’s a direction the company teased just weeks back during the Goodwood Festival of Speed, when it restored Bruce McLaren’s personal M6 GT—a Can-Am machine essentially rebodied with a closed cockpit for Le Mans and the like, that never actually competed and was ultimately converted into a road car. That M6 GT is essentially a blueprint for what McLaren seems to want to achieve with this machine, with the benefit of another half-century of technological progress and refinement to pull from. Sign us up.

item.text:
Media | Articles
2026 Hyundai Santa Fe XRT Review: New Niche Unlocked
Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.
Get automotive news, DIY tips, market trends, in-depth car profiles, and more right in your email inbox.
With 83.5% of new-vehicle sales accounted for by SUVs, vans, and trucks, you might think that we’ve exhausted all possible variations on the crossover theme. Wrong, says Hyundai Motor Group. The conglomerate that saw into the three-row-loving hearts of America’s middle class with the Telluride/Palisade has discovered another niche Americans didn’t know they liked: The affordable three-row SUV that isn’t too big. The fifth-generation Santa Fe is executing this formula with modernist style and a butch flair with great success. The sales figures suggest that bigger is not always better, because last year the Santa Fe outsold its bigger brother, the Palisade (and Telluride), posting the best-ever year for the model.
Four years ago, the Santa Fe was swoopy and generic-looking. The fifth-generation, which debuted for the 2024 model year, was boxy and truck-like. The look was the biggest difference: It wasn’t much larger—stretching two inches longer overall with a two-inch longer wheelbase—and it wasn’t terribly different under the sheetmetal, using the same platform as the fourth-gen car adopted for its 2021 facelift. Stiffer, lighter, and stronger than the Y7 it replaced, the N3 platform signaled the end of the problematic Theta II engine in the Santa Fe and allowed for a more spacious interior. The big news for the 2026 model year is the transmission: Hyundai swapped the problematic eight-speed dual-clutch transmission (DCT) for a traditional torque-converter automatic with the same number of speeds.
We tested the AWD-only XRT trim, which falls smack in the middle of the Santa Fe range. For 2026, it comes with Terrain Mode, which allows you to select different profiles for Mud, Snow, and Sand. Other XRT-specific features include a 4500-lb (vs. 3500-lb) towing capacity (as long as your trailer has brakes), all-terrain tires, and an additional 1.3 inches of ground clearance. Our tester wore Earth Brown Brass paint ($1000) and carpeted floor mats ($240). The out-the-door price was $44,525. (Current shoppers will note that the base price has changed slightly: For 2027, the same vehicle will cost you $45,180 out the door.)
Specs: 2026 Hyundai Santa Fe XRT
• Price: $43,285/$44,525 (base / as-tested 2026 model)
• Powertrain: 2.5-liter turbocharged inline-four, eight-speed automatic transmission 
• Horsepower: 277 @ 5800 rpm
• Torque: 311 @ 4000 rpm
• Layout: Three-row, seven-passenger crossover
• Weight: 4486 pounds
• EPA-Rated Fuel Economy: 19/25/21 (city/hwy/combined)
• 0–60 mph: ~7 seconds (est.)
• Competitors: Kia Sorento X-Pro, Nissan Pathfinder Rock Creek
Though the modernist details are pure Hyundai, the Santa Fe’s silhouette recalls some familiar models. The blunt nose, gently raked roofline, and ride height are reminiscent of the Ford Explorer, which also uses pronounced fender flares and side contours to project a muscular air. The shape of the wheel openings, shrouded in black plastic, are very Subaru. The eight-bit flair of the light signatures is all Hyundai, however—and we dig it. Blistered and bulging, with a face that is both human and friendly, the fifth-gen Santa Fe looks absolutely nothing like the car it replaced. The visual is not timelessly beautiful, but perhaps it is too soon to cast a verdict on how the Santa Fe will age. Heck, the Studebaker Avanti was super weird, and that hasn’t stopped people from adoring it decades later.
The interior, in contrast to the outside, is designed with clean, straight lines. It doesn’t feel expensive, but it also doesn’t feel as cut-rate as the cabin of a Subaru, for instance. Design has definitely become Korea’s forte (sorry). Though the cabin of our XRT doesn’t use any upscale materials, the metal-look plastics have interesting textures and that “H” motif is everywhere. One of the few places it is not present is the steering wheel, which doesn’t bear a badge at all, just a blank piece of silver plastic. It makes you wonder: How much would it have cost to mold it with “Hyundai”?
The “tall, three-row SUV” form factor is successful for a reason. Adults fit very comfortably in the second row, and those we chauffeured, who ranged in height from petite to six feet, remarked on the conveniently placed bag hooks and the charging ports. The third row is very cramped (only two seats). We don’t hold this against Hyundai, because—as a marketer for a major OEM once acknowledged in a press briefing—three-row SUV buyers don’t frequently use the third row; they just like to know it’s there. If you frequently carry adults in the third row, you are far more likely to choose a minivan. Plus, look how tiny the Santa Fe’s trunk is with the third row upright! You could fit seven people’s toothbrushes back there, and that’s about it.
The fifth-gen Santa Fe relies on an all-aluminum, 277-hp, 2.5-liter turbocharged engine from Hyundai’s “Smartstream” engine family. The 2.5-liter uses direct and port fuel injection, and continuously variable valve timing and valve duration. Power is adequate, though the nearly 4500-pound SUV does not feel quick. The transmission feels busy under enthusiastic acceleration, so the smoother you are with application, the less inclined it is to pop through the gears. Thankfully, the engine is quiet and not as groany as most four-cylinders.
The steering-column-mounted shifter, essentially a stalk with a rotating end piece, takes a little getting used to, but we didn’t have any “yikes” moments, and we found neutral on the first try. We expect most customers will be happy to trade the traditional lever or rotary dial for more space for phones and cupholders. The main wrinkle with the driving experience was the lane-centering (when using Highway Driving Assist), which was particularly twitchy with its corrections.
The 2026 Santa Fe uses Hyundai’s connected car Navigation Cockpit (CCNC) infotainment system, which can do all sorts of fancy things like accept payments and read your fingerprint. The system will get higher-tech soon: This is the last model year before the Santa Fe switches to Pleos Connect, which uses an Android Auto operating system, integrates advanced artificial intelligence, and combines “a central widescreen with physical buttons.” We’re curious to know the extent of the physical-button usage: Our tester uses a mix of touchscreen controls and physical buttons for HVAC, volume, cameras, and seek/track functions, which was fine most of the time. You can make the cabin warmer/cooler without looking and simply reaching for the knob, but if you want to turn on defrost or the seat heaters, you have to look down to find it, then tap the little icon.
Though there are three-row SUVs aplenty, and many of them have off-road packages, the size and cost of the 2026 Santa Fe XRT place it in a surprisingly small group. It’s easy to find three-row SUVs bigger than this. It’s hard to find three rows in this “tweener” size. It’s even harder to find ones that look fresh, from a design perspective (case in point: Nissan’s Pathfinder Rock Creek). A low cost also sets apart the Santa Fe XRT: Ford, GM, Honda, and Toyota all offer three-row SUVs with more robust off-road kit—but they cost significantly more. Even the Subaru Ascent, which aligns with the Santa Fe’s budget-minded ethos and one-ups it with full-time AWD and a 5000-pound towing capacity, is different in an important metric: Size. You can get a lot of truck for $45K, but you’ll have a very hard time finding a rugged-looking SUV with three rows of seats and an overall length under 16 feet.
The Santa Fe XRT is best suited for budget-minded buyers who find its size “just right” and prioritize design over off-road kit. One note to those who may be shopping used: Hyundai’s trademark 10-year/100,000-mile powertrain warranty only applies to the vehicle under its original owner and to certified pre-owned examples. If the vehicle isn’t CPO by Hyundai, those terms change to five years/60,000 miles. So far, the Smartstream engines seem to be less trouble-prone than their Theta predecessors (as one would hope), but the warranty terms are worth being aware of, especially if you’re starstruck by the sticker price.
In our week with the Santa Fe XRT, we came to see why this three-row SUV has found such sales success in the United States. People like this size SUV for its high driving position, spacious second row, and maneuverable footprint, and Hyundai sweetens the deal with distinctive, fresh styling and an interior that feels current in design and tech. We remain curious how many of these we’ll see on the road in five or ten years, but for now, Hyundai’s Goldilocks-sized three-row is enjoying its moment as the cool kid.

2027 Hyundai Elantra Is Bigger, More Powerful, And Gets Up To 53 MPG
The new Elantra grows 3.4 inches and introduces a more powerful hybrid powertrain targeting up to 53 MPG combined.
The Hyundai Elantra is getting a major overhaul for 2027. That means a bigger size, more power, and a whole bunch of fresh tech. Hyundai debuted the eighth-generation Elantra at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show, including the Elantra Hybrid, which will hit the market in 2028.
The new Elantra adopts Hyundai's Art of Steel design language, which brings sharper styling and more muscular proportions to the compact sedan. It's also larger than the outgoing model, with a longer wheelbase that Hyundai says creates more rear-seat space.
Both gasoline and hybrid versions will be available in the US. The standard 2027 Elantra goes on sale first, while the 2028 Elantra Hybrid will follow. Hyundai hasn't announced pricing or specific launch dates for either model.
2027 Hyundai Elantra
The eighth-generation Elantra introduces Hyundai's Art of Steel design philosophy to the compact sedan segment. The new look emphasizes wider fenders, a longer hood, and more traditional three-box proportions, giving the car a wider, more athletic appearance.
It's also noticeably larger than the outgoing model. The new Elantra measures 188.8 inches long, 73.0 inches wide, and 56.1 inches tall. Its 108.3-inch wheelbase is 1.2 inches longer than before. Here are the specifics:
- Length: 188.8 inches (+3.4 inches)
- Width: 73.0 inches (+1.2 inches)
- Height: 56.1 inches
- Wheelbase: 108.3 inches (+1.2 inches)
- Coefficient of drag: 0.26
That added size means more room for passengers in the rear. Hyundai says the new Elantra has best-in-class rear passenger space, with dimensions that approach those of some mid-size sedans.
Rear legroom measures 39.1 inches, while rear headroom comes in at 37.7 inches. Rear shoulder room is 56.5 inches. Slimmer front seat frames also help create additional space for passengers in the second row.
Other practical additions include rear air vents, standard USB-C charging ports, and an available 60/40 split-folding rear seatback. Hyundai says the cabin can accommodate adults and front- or rear-facing child seats.
The standard 2027 Elantra uses a familiar 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine, though Hyundai has made several updates to improve efficiency and refinement. The Atkinson-cycle Smartstream engine produces an estimated 147 horsepower and 132 pound-feet of torque.
Power goes to the front wheels through Hyundai's Intelligent Variable Transmission (IVT) with Shiftronic. The automaker has also revised the transmission with a wider ratio range and reduced internal friction. Here’s what the full specs look like:
- Engine: 2.0-liter Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder
- Output: 147 hp
- Torque: 132 lb-ft
- Transmission: Intelligent Variable Transmission with Shiftronic
- Drivetrain: Front-wheel drive
- Targeted fuel economy: Up to 35 mpg combined
Hyundai is targeting up to 35 mpg combined for gasoline-powered models equipped with 16-inch wheels. EPA ratings will arrive closer to the car's US launch.
The 2028 Elantra Hybrid gets a more substantial powertrain upgrade. It retains a 1.6-liter four-cylinder hybrid setup but increases combined system output from 139 to 155 horsepower.
The electric motor now produces 45 kilowatts, up from 32 kW in the previous model. Hyundai also enlarged the high-voltage battery from 1.32 to 1.49 kilowatt-hours.
Unlike many hybrids that use continuously variable transmissions, the Elantra Hybrid pairs its powertrain with a six-speed dual-clutch transmission. It also gets a multi-link independent rear suspension, replacing the torsion-beam setup found in the gasoline model. Here’s what those specs look like:
- Engine: 1.6-liter four-cylinder hybrid
- Combined output: 155 hp
- Electric motor output: 45 kW
- Battery capacity: 1.49 kWh
- Transmission: Six-speed dual-clutch
- Drivetrain: Front-wheel drive
- Targeted fuel economy: Up to 53 mpg combined
The redesigned cabin introduces Hyundai's Pleos Connect infotainment platform, which is based on Android Automotive OS. It centers around a standard 12.9-inch Full HD touchscreen and brings a more customizable, smartphone-like interface to the Elantra.
The system includes wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, Bluelink connected services, SiriusXM, Wi-Fi capability, and over-the-air software updates.
There's also a new Gleo AI voice assistant, which uses a large language model to understand natural-language commands. Hyundai says the system supports contextual conversations, multiple commands, and voice recognition for both drivers and passengers.
Importantly, Hyundai hasn't abandoned physical controls. Frequently used functions, including audio and climate settings, retain dedicated buttons and knobs. Higher trims also offer heated and ventilated front seats, a power driver's seat with memory, ambient interior lighting, and a power moonroof.
Hyundai will offer the 2027 Elantra in three gasoline-powered trims: SE, SEL Sport, and Limited. The 2028 Elantra Hybrid will also have three configurations: SE Blue, SEL Sport Hybrid, and Limited Hybrid.
Pricing, final EPA fuel economy ratings, and US launch dates haven't been announced. Hyundai says those details will arrive closer to the vehicles' respective on-sale dates. But with more interior space, updated technology, and a hybrid promising up to 53 mpg, it all sounds promising.

item.title: This Abandoned Range Rover Sat For 5 Years. Then They Brought It Back To Life
item.text:
This Abandoned Range Rover Sat For 5 Years. Then They Brought It Back To Life
WD Detailing revives a mold-covered 1992 Range Rover, restoring the interior and waking its 3.9-liter V8 after five dormant years.
Mark's son Cody got a Range Rover for his sixteenth birthday. Cody died in a 2011 accident, and the SUV sat untouched for five years, parked under a walnut tree before it moved to a friend's lot for another six months.
The crew at WD Detailing found a 1992 Range Rover buried in mold, dead grass growing through the wheels, and grease baked onto the hood. They didn't know the full story until Mark showed up and explained why the truck had been left to rot.
The restoration started with hardware. Rusted bolts held a tow bar to the front bumper. The crew needed a wrench and an impact driver just to break them loose before washing could even begin.
The rear carrier wouldn't budge either. The pin had rusted solid inside the hitch, so the team strapped the basket for safety and cut through it with a rotary tool instead of fighting the corrosion by hand.
Paint correction meant wet sanding the hood before the first wash, since organic growth had etched into the clear coat itself. The EPA's own guidance on basic mold cleanup steps notes that moldy porous material often has to be discarded rather than cleaned. That's why the carpets came out entirely instead of getting scrubbed in place.
Interior work followed the same pattern: vacuum first to pull loose dirt, then hot water extraction, then steam to break down stains baked into the seats. The EPA also notes that cleanup under roughly 10 square feet can typically be handled without a professional. This job ran well past that scale.
Abandoned 1992 Range Rover Covered In Mold
Under the hood sits a 3.9-liter V8 making 180 horsepower and 227 pound-feet of torque. It's an aluminum-block engine Rover bought the rights to from GM back in the 1960s. Five years of sitting dormant left it without spark or injector pulse when the team's mechanic, Adam, first turned the key.
Adam traced the dead injectors to a failed ignition module, the part that signals the coil to fire and tells the computer when to pulse the injectors. A dead fuel pump compounded the problem. He installed a replacement and ran fresh fuel lines to the front of the engine.
Plenty of Range Rover Classics get rescued with full rebuilds or modern engine swaps, chasing more power or long-haul reliability. This one stayed closer to its roots.
Once the new pump kicked on and the ignition module fed a clean signal, the original V8 fired and settled into a steady idle. After five silent years, the truck crept forward and back under its own power again before the crew finished the final polish.
Source: WD Detailing

item.title: Over 1 Million Honda And Acura Vehicles Face Start/Stop Failure That Could Leave Drivers Stranded
item.text:
Over 1 Million Honda And Acura Vehicles Face Start/Stop Failure That Could Leave Drivers Stranded
NHTSA's EA26007 focuses on Auto Start/Stop failures in recent Honda and Acura models, without yet triggering a formal safety recall.
Honda and Acura owners who have noticed the engine won't fire back up at a red light aren't imagining things. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened a new engineering analysis covering more than a million of the vehicles.
The agency's opening documents list 701 owner complaints when the investigation was opened. Drivers describe the Auto Start/Stop system shutting the engine off at a complete stop, then failing to restart it when they take a foot off the brake.
NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26007 covers an estimated 1,033,632 vehicles. The agency says it opened the probe "to determine the scope and severity of the potential issue and assess any associated safety risks."
2025 Honda Odyssey
The investigation spans the 2024-2026 Honda Odyssey, Passport, Ridgeline, and Pilot, plus the 2024-2026 Acura MDX. All five share the same Auto Start/Stop feature that cuts the engine at stoplights to save fuel.
EA26007 sits alongside EA25004, a separate engineering analysis NHTSA opened in 2025. That one examines similar Auto Start/Stop failures in specific 2016-2025 Honda Pilot, 2018-2025 Odyssey, 2019-2025 Passport, 2020-2025 Ridgeline, 2015-2025 Acura TLX, and 2016-2025 Acura MDX models.
NHTSA's summary for the new analysis lists no crashes, fires, injuries, or fatalities tied to the 701 complaints.
Neither Honda nor Acura has issued a recall for this condition. An engineering analysis is NHTSA's tool for digging into a pattern of complaints before deciding whether a defect exists and a recall is warranted.
Service documents tied to the earlier EA25004 probe describe the mechanism. Under certain conditions, excessive cylinder pressure or low cranking torque keeps the engine from restarting after Auto Idle Stop engages.
The listed workaround is shifting to Park and pressing the ENGINE START/STOP button.
2024 Honda Ridgeline Trailsport
Honda and Acura have issued service bulletins 26-090 and 26-019 ahead of NHTSA's new analysis. The Acura bulletin applies to 2016-2020 MDX models except Hybrid, 2022-2026 MDX models except Type S, and 2015-2020 TLX V6 sedans that show the same restart symptoms. Actual coverage is defined by VIN and build data.
The bulletins target three symptoms: the engine not restarting automatically after idle stop, slow cranking, and failure to start in hot ambient conditions. Earlier countermeasures on related Honda and Acura models combined a PGM-FI software update with starter assembly, starter-relay, or valve-adjustment work where needed.
Acura's own service communication warns that replacement parts are available only in limited quantities. Repairs are being prioritized for vehicles already showing symptoms, and owners are being told to temporarily disable Auto Idle Stop in the meantime.
Internal dealer guidance points to broader owner notification on the Acura bulletin starting as early as late December 2026. The public bulletin only commits to notifying owners once sufficient parts are available. Until that happens, most affected owners won't get a direct heads-up.
Source: NHTSA

item.title: Honda Avancier Debuts As A New 7-Seat Hybrid
item.text:
Honda Avancier Debuts As A New 7-Seat Hybrid
The new SUV debuts a bold new design
This is the Honda Avancier, and no, it isn't something you'll be able to buy in America. Instead, this three-row, seven-seat SUV is a new flagship model for Japan, Southeast Asia, and Australia that slots above the popular CR-V. It's also important as it's the first model underpinned by Honda's new mid-size hybrid platform and includes its next-generation hybrid powertrain.
The Avancier looks like nothing else in Honda's current range. It's based on what Honda calls the 'Grand-Journey' concept and, frankly, has very little traditional Honda DNA. Look at the front, and you'll immediately notice Honda's new 'H' logo and the lack of a traditional grille. Instead, there are two smaller intakes positioned at the front. As is the trend nowadays, the Avancier also has split headlights with sharp DRLs just below the line of the hood. The headlamps are then positioned further down.
Honda's bold design theme continues along the sides of the Avancier with black rocker panels, flush door angles, and thick, angled D-pillars. The back might be the SUV's most dramatic angle. It includes vertical taillights and a full-width LED light bar. There's also a spoiler stretching out from the roof, which hides the rear wiper.
A brand-new platform
Beneath the skin of the Avancier is a new mid-size platform that will support vehicles across the C- and D-segments, including SUVs and sedans. The platform includes a large area directly under the cockpit to house the exhaust components and the hybrid's battery packs. Areas of the new platform are stiffer than before, while other sections are less stiff, and Honda says this new design helps to increase the tire's contact patch and delivers smoother load transfer while cornering. Honda has used approximately 40% more high-tensile steel while simultaneously reducing weight from its outgoing platform.
The Avancier comes standard with Honda's Motion Management System found in other vehicles and, in a Honda first, the SUV includes its new DualPower eAWD system where electric motors at the front and rear independently control each axle.
Honda goes all-in on hybrid power
Speaking of power, the Honda Avancier is the brand's first model with its new mid-size hybrid powertrain, which is also coming to the new CR-V. It uses a new 2.0-liter four-cylinder that aims to ensure every bit of fuel injected into the cylinder is combusted. To make this happen, Honda altered the shape of the intake port so it's shaped like a ski jump, increasing airflow velocity and working alongside a two-piece water jacket cooling the exhaust port from both sides. Engineers have also changed the shape of the piston crowns to speed up the combustion process. The engine is roughly 900 grams lighter than Honda's outgoing 2.0-liter, thanks largely to a new crankshaft that's 500 grams lighter. All of this engine work is said to improve efficiency and performance.
Improvements have also been made to the electric motors. They are now lighter, and the drive motors use magnets free of heavy rare-earth materials. The same S+ Shift function as the Prelude and Civic e:HEV RS has also been included. Honda hasn't said how much power this new hybrid system delivers, other than revealing the rear-mounted motor has 50 kW. It's also not yet ready to announce efficiency details, though we expect to see these important details announced soon.
A fresh new Honda cabin
The Avancier also launches with a big new interior design. It has a large new infotainment screen perched on top of the dashboard and a digital instrument cluster as standard. It's not these screens that are the most dramatic feature, however. That would have to be the all-new steering wheel that has a completely flat bottom and includes new controls for the media and cruise control.
There's a fresh dashboard, too, trimmed in plush leather and complete with ambient lighting. The door panels are relatively simple, each includes a strip of lighting, and a large transmission tunnel sits between the front occupants. A column shifter has been added.
As this is a big SUV, it's perhaps the second row that's more important than the front. It has a spacious bench seat and a fold-down armrest that houses a touch display for the climate control and the heated and ventilated seats. The Avancier also includes power-operated sunshades in the second row. As standard, the SUV includes a 12-speaker Bose premium audio system with Dolby Atmos, a Remote In-Cabin View camera, and an advanced voice recognition system. Other features include a panoramic glass roof and rear privacy glass. All Avancier models will support over-the-air software updates.
The Avancier is one of the first of Honda's 15 next-generation hybrid models launching by the end of March 2030, which will also include the new CR-V heading to the United States. As we recently reported, that new model will share its mid-size platform with the Avancier and use the same 2.0-liter hybrid powertrain.

item.title: AC Cobra
item.text:
The AC Cobra, sold in the United States as the Shelby Cobra and Shelby AC Cobra, is a sports car manufactured by British company AC Cars, with a Ford V8 engine. It was produced intermittently in both the United Kingdom and later the United States from 1962 to 1967.


== History and development ==
AC Cars had been building small numbers of its AC Ace two-seater roadster since 1953. The Ace had a steel ladder chassis with 3-inch (76 mm) diameter tubular main rails, and a hand-built body of aluminium panels shaped using English wheeling machines. The Ace had used three different straight-six engines over its production life, starting with AC's own Light Six, then Bristol Cars six derived from the pre-war BMW M328, and finally a 2.6 L (160 cu in) Ford Zephyr 6 engine. The Zephyr 6 was low enough that it allowed AC to restyle the nose of the car, lowering the hoodline, adding a smaller air intake, and removing the "moustache" lines below the headlamps on earlier cars.
In September 1961, Ford provided Shelby with two of its new 221 cu in (3.6 L) small block V8 engines, one of which was shipped to AC in England.


== AC Ace 3.6 ==
In January 1962 mechanics at AC Cars in Thames Ditton, Surrey completed the "AC Ace 3.6" prototype with chassis number CSX2000.
AC had already made most of the modifications needed for the small-block V8 when they installed the Ford Zephyr 6 engine, including the extensive rework of the AC Ace's front end bodywork. The only modification of the front end of the first Cobra from that of the "AC Ace 2.6" was the steering box, which had to be moved outward to clear the wider V8 engine.
A significant modification was the fitting of a stronger rear differential to handle the increased engine power. In the place of the old E.N.V. unit was a Salisbury 4HU differential with inboard disc brakes to reduce unsprung weight—the same unit used on the Jaguar E-Type.
After testing and modification, the engine and transmission were removed and the chassis was air-freighted to Shelby in Los Angeles on 2 February 1962.
By this time the small-block's displacement was increased to 4.3 L (260 cu in). Shelby's team installed the engine and a transmission into CSX2000 in less than eight hours at Dean Moon's shop in Santa Fe Springs, California, and began road-testing.


== Production ==
(CSX/CS 2001–2602)
A few changes were made to the production version:

The inboard brakes were moved outboard to reduce cost.
The fuel tank filler was relocated from the fender to the center of the trunk. The trunk lid had to be shortened to accommodate this change.
AC exported completed, painted, and trimmed cars (less engine and gearbox) to Shelby who then finished the cars in his workshop in Los Angeles by installing the engine and gearbox and correcting any bodywork flaws caused by the car's passage by sea. A small number of cars were also completed on the East Coast of the US by Ed Hugus in Pennsylvania, including the first production car; CSX2001.
The first 75 Cobra Mk1 models (including the prototype) were fitted with the 4.3 L (260 cu in) Windsor Ford V8. The remaining 51 Mk1 models were fitted with the larger 4.7-litre (289 cu in) version of the engine. After the 289 became available, Shelby offered an upgrade to the earlier cars. Most accepted the upgrade so cars with the 260 CID engine are rare today.
In late 1962, Alan Turner, AC's chief engineer, completed a major design change of the car's front end to accommodate rack and pinion steering while still using transverse leaf spring suspension (with the leaf spring doubling as the upper suspension link). The new car entered production in early 1963 and was designated Mark II. The steering rack was borrowed from the MGB while the new steering column came from the VW Beetle. About 528 Mark II Cobras were produced from 1963 to the summer of 1965. The last US-bound Mark II was produced in November 1964.


== European model ==
(COB/COX 6001–6062)
The Ace 2.6 was discontinued in 1963 to keep production focused on building cars for Shelby American Inc. To supply cars to the European market, AC began to market and sell the Cobra in Europe. Advertisements from the time state that the Cobra was designed to meet the requirements of Shelby American Inc.


== Chassis CSX2196 (the "Flip Top" Cobra) ==
Shelby experimented with a 390-cubic-inch (6.4 L) Ford FE engine in chassis CSX2196. The car did not receive the development it needed, as all available resources were committed to taking the crown from Ferrari in the GT class. Ken Miles raced the FE-powered Mark II at Sebring and pronounced the car virtually undrivable, naming it "The Turd". The car retired early with a failed engine.
However, the car was not just "virtually undriveable"; during the earlier practice session at Sebring, Ken had lost control of CSX2196 and crashed into a tree. After the disastrous race, with crash damage to repair and wild handling to improve, the car was completely stripped. Rebuilding the car from the bottom up, significant changes were made to the chassis and bodywork. The chassis was strengthened and stiffened to handle the greater power and torque of larger engines, using the same techniques as employed on the Shelby Daytona Coupe. The bodywork had to facilitate easier access to engine, drivetrain and suspension, so clamshells were installed front and rear, pivoting at the extremities and earning CSX2196 the nickname "Flip Top" Cobra. In addition to clamshells, the doors were hinged along the bottom and flipped down to open.
The revised CSX2196 raced in the showdown at Nassau, where a more relaxed division of racing classes allowed the Cobras to run against a prototype Ford GT40, GM Grand Sport Corvettes and a Lola Mk6. An aluminium 6.4-litre (390 cu in) engine was used. By the end of the first lap, the Cobra had a lead the length of the start-finish straight. However, the car failed to finish due to brake problems.
CSX2196 never raced again, remaining as a one-off development prototype, but it had proven a point - a big-block powered Cobra had huge potential, and the lessons learned facilitated production of the Cobra 427.
The car itself survives today, being driven occasionally at international prestige and enthusiast meetings.


== Cobra 427 ==

A new chassis, designated Mark III, was designed in cooperation with Ford in Detroit. The Mark III chassis was built using 101.6 mm (4 in) main chassis tubes, up from 76.2 mm (3 in), and coil spring suspension all around (an especially significant change up front, where the previously used transverse leaf spring had done double duty as the top link). The new car also had wide fenders and a larger radiator opening. It was powered by the Ford 7.0 L (427 cu in) FE "side oiler" engine equipped with a single 4-barrel 780 CFM Holley carburetor rated at 317 kW (425 hp; 431 PS) at 6000 rpm and 651 N⋅m (480 lb⋅ft) at 3700 rpm of torque, which provided a top speed of 264 km/h (164 mph) in the standard model. item.text:
The Integrated Transport Centre (Abu Dhabi Mobility) has launched special vehicle number plates featuring the Liwa International Festival 2027 (LIWA 2027) logo.
The plates give motorists a new way to mark the festival, which will take place in the Al Dhafra Region from 11 December 2026 until 2 January 2027. Liwa International Festival is one of the UAE’s leading heritage and sporting events, bringing together cultural, community and competitive activities.
The new number plates feature a design combining the festival’s red logo with the Abu Dhabi emblem and vehicle registration number. The plates are available in both short and long formats.
Vehicle owners can obtain the festival-themed number plates at designated service centres across Abu Dhabi. These include the main Driver and Vehicle Licensing Sector building and Al Salama building in Abu Dhabi City, the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Centre in Falaj Hazza in Al Ain Region, and the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Centre in Bada Zayed in the Al Dhafra Region.
His Excellency Dr Abdulla Hamad Al Ghfeli, Director General of the Integrated Transport Centre, said: “The launch of these number plates reflects the centre’s commitment to providing services that respond to the interests of community members and offer new opportunities to participate in prominent occasions and events. This initiative also enables vehicle owners to express their connection to Liwa International Festival and celebrate its distinctive identity as one of the UAE’s leading heritage and sporting events.”
For more information on how to obtain the new number plates visit admobility.gov.ae or contact the Department of Municipalities and Transport’s Service Support Centre on the toll-free number 800850.

item.title: REO Trucks Speed Into the Next Phase of Life - Hagerty Media
item.text:
Media | Articles
REO Trucks Speed Into the Next Phase of Life
Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.
Get automotive news, DIY tips, market trends, in-depth car profiles, and more right in your email inbox.
It was a simple promise, one of a body-on-frame pickup with modesty as its selling point. The dimensions are tidy. There’s a mandatory four-cylinder engine, with no cost or maintenance concerns from the addition of forced induction or direct injection. The engine is teamed up with a manual or automatic gearbox, and the body is designed by the legendary Frank Stephenson, whose name has graced the designs of Ferraris, McLarens, and the new Mini. Now we have more information, a handful of digital renderings, and a trio of affordable price tags for what could be the most perfect truck in decades.
Stephenson and his design company were given the task of designing a simple and cost-effective vehicle with three unique body styles atop the same 119.6-inch wheelbase, sharing DNA upstream of REO’s corporate B-pillar and corporate front end. That fascia has a bit of a Jeep Cherokee (XJ) look, with a large but understated grille set within a subtly chiseled nose. There are stacked headlights akin to a squarebody Chevy truck, or the XJ Cherokee Wagoneer, if you want to get picky. The bumper looks like an aftermarket steel affair from Ranch Hand, though it and items like the door panels, headliner, and trim are supposedly removable in under five minutes with common tools.
We discussed REO and its CEO in a previous story this summer, before we sampled a Slate EV truck and heard about Ford’s upcoming Fathom. But we now have more details on REO’s three products, and this latest news suggests all derivations remain true to what made them set social media on fire this summer: open-source repair information, no software locks, no subscriptions, no traditional car dealerships, and readily available factory and aftermarket parts.
While no interior or production details are provided, the exterior insights on each REO vehicle are certainly appealing. And worth a closer look:
Runabout T4X – $21,500 (estimated)
The cheapest REO is a regular cab work truck with two seats, a separate 6.5-foot bed, and a massive B-pillar. This is significantly different from a Slate EV, which utilizes a unitized body and a 5-foot bed that theoretically cannot handle the same payload weight. A separate bed is less likely to damage the entire truck under load, as the renderings suggest a painted metal body over the Slate’s plastic construction. The bed also features a dropside design, with a flat floor, much like those rigs you rent from Home Depot or what’s commonplace in the Japanese Kei truck market.
An enclosed storage nook rests between the cab and the rear axle, suggesting this rig can be ready for just about any activity a compact truck can handle. REO estimates a base price of $21,500, which is thousands less than the Slate EV. REO is targeting a 5000lb tow rating, 22-25 miles per gallon (combined city and highway), a 500-600-mile range, and a lofty powertrain life of 500,000 miles.
There is a Ransom edition (named after Ransom Olds, natch) that’s akin to a Z71 Chevy, a TRD Toyota, or an FX4 Ford. A taller ride height and more aggressive shocks are expected, and the Ransom has better approach (42.5° / 48.3°), departure (17.4° / 20.5°), and breakover (16.3° / 21.2°) angles than a stock REO.
Runabout T4C – $25,000 (estimated)
This four-door Runabout T4C has a significantly different body than the T4X, suggesting the addition of two more doors turns this truck into a single-body affair like the 2001-2013 Chevrolet Avalanche. This configuration has five seats with two rows, and an overall length shorter by about an inch (195.6 inches). REO suggests this rig will tow the same 5000 lbs, but payload capacities are still unknown.
All REOs share the same wheelbase, and these renderings suggest this makes the rear doors as tight around the legs as the aforementioned XJ Jeep Cherokee. The bed no longer drops down, and it’s deep enough to mandate bumps for the wheel arches. The Runabout T4C is estimated to have a $25,000 base price.
Runabout S4C – $28,500 (estimated)
And if the previous model was a Chevy Avalanche, the Runabout S4C is a Chevy Tahoe incarnate. This REO seats six passengers via the addition of a jump seat. The latter throne is likely similar to the cramped affairs of extended-cab Rangers and S-10s of the past, as this fully enclosed SUV has a shorter overall length (182.7 inches) than the T4C. There is a lockable storage compartment opposite the jump seat, and the significantly larger interior is likely the primary reason why this is the most expensive REO at $28,500.
With these prices and REO’s proud proclamation of internal combustion motivation, this Texas startup appears to offer a significant value proposition. In theory, REO is courting everyone from the traditional side-by-side powersports customer to those looking at Kei trucks, be it older examples or the new Scion Kei-01. While pricing for the Scion isn’t known as of yet, odds are Toyota’s penchant for premium pricing will likely put it ahead of the REO.
The other genre of players in this space is electrified, and currently occupied by the Slate EV truck and the upcoming Ford Fathom. Both EVs are likely to be more car-like, as the Slate I sampled was downright El Camino-like in body construction, and Ford’s electric trucklet is the first offering of a chassis intended for a whole class of affordable vehicles. But Slate is far ahead of the game, with prototypes and a promise to begin deliveries in Q1 2027. The theoretical Ford isn’t far behind, and it’s unlikely to disappear after a 2 billion dollar Kentucky commitment to a Universal EV platform.
There’s a lot to like about REO and their trio of trucks. But it’s worth tempering your excitement for at least a moment: they are currently a private company with no listed investors, unlike all the Amazon alumni-backed hoopla around Slate. That name recognition lent Slate an air of financial stability that REO currently lacks; however, REO says they’ve taken over 40,000 paid reservations for their product. At $25 (refundable, too), that potentially put a million bucks into their coffers. If true, that could provide adequate incentive for well-heeled private investors to also cut them a check. REO has been pretty silent about that matter, but Expedition Portal suggests they have backing from the likes of “automotive suppliers, logistics industry executives, and several Midwest manufacturing firms.”
Whether or not REO is a going concern is anyone’s guess at the moment, but there’s no doubt they are using all the right words. And they certainly got Frank Stephenson to whip them up an honest-looking little truck for the job.

Aston Martin Headed to Dakar with Dreadnought and Fernando Alonso
Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.
Get automotive news, DIY tips, market trends, in-depth car profiles, and more right in your email inbox.
When it made its debut earlier in 2026, the Aston Martin Dreadnought was presented as a virtual concept designed for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. It’s about to exit the digital world and land in one of the most unforgiving races on the planet. Aston Martin Racing has announced that it will compete in the Dakar Rally for the first time with three examples of the Dreadnought.
Aston Martin developed the Dakar-bound Dreadnought with the help of Prodrive, a race engineering company that has worked closely with the British brand’s endurance racing team for over 20 years. Don’t look for DBX underpinnings here: The off-roader is a true, purpose-designed rally car that shares nothing with Aston Martin’s production models. The renderings released by the firm show a buggy-like racer with huge tires, a generous amount of ground clearance, and extreme approach and departure angles.
The styling evolved considerably as the Dreadnought made the leap from your monitor to the dunes. While the original concept almost reminded us of classic Aston Martin models, the rally car headed to Dakar is characterized by a function-over-form design drawn around off-road capability, cooling, and aerodynamics. Only the shape of the hood and the rear spoiler hint that it’s an Aston.
Specifications haven’t been released, though it looks like the Dreadnought is powered by a mid-mounted engine. It takes more than raw power to win Dakar, however, so Aston Martin has recruited a star-studded lineup of drivers for the race. One car will be given to Fernando Alonso, who currently drives for Aston Martin’s Formula 1 team. He’s a two-time Formula 1 world champion, and he won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2018 and 2019. Another will be driven by nine-time WRC winner Sébastien Loeb, while the third will be in the hands of reigning FIA World Rally Raid champion Lucas Moraes. All three pilots have previously raced in the Dakar.
The 2027 Dakar Rally will take place from January 9 to 23. It starts in the south of Portugal, heads across southern Spain, and goes into Morocco, where most of the race takes place. This will be the first time that the Dakar Rally is held in Africa since 2007, and the route sounds like a tough one. It includes over 2600 miles of special stages through the Atlas Mountains and the Sahara Desert.

item.title: 2026 GRMN Corolla First Drive: An Even Madder Smile Machine - Hagerty Media
item.text:
Media | Articles
2026 GRMN Corolla First Drive: An Even Madder Smile Machine
Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.
Get automotive news, DIY tips, market trends, in-depth car profiles, and more right in your email inbox.
“Spicy-boy turbomonkey.” “Full chihuahua.” “An utterly ridiculous pop rock.” These are a few of the phrases coined by our editorial staff when we spent a day at Barber Motorsports Park with the 2023 GR Corolla (specifically, the Morizo Edition). Three and a half years have passed, and the wonderful people who designed this riotous three-cylinder hatchback have not left well enough alone. We got chassis and aero tweaks (2024), an automatic transmission (2025), more power for the base car, plus more chassis upgrades (2026), and most recently a new model with the most intense, track-focused upgrades yet. That version wears the hallowed letters GRMN, which stand for Gazoo Racing Masters of Nürburgring, a track that’s central to its story and to that of Gazoo Racing. As of last week, we’ve had a chance to drive it on track, and even after a brief stint, it’s clear that Toyota’s mad smile machine has gotten even more fun.
After five years of tutelage under Toyota’s late chief test driver Hiromu Naruse, Toyota CEO Akio Toyoda started racing (using a pseudonym) at the 24 Hours of Nürburgring in 2007. (He returned in 2009, 2014, 2016, and 2019, as well.) Since 2009, Toyota has used the GRMN badge to designate high-performance, limited-edition versions of various models for its home market in Japan. Toyoda’s pseudonym, Morizo, now graces the other high-performance version of the GR Corolla.
Though it is lighter, stiffer, and offers more oomph than the base GR Corolla, the GRMN was not born of a desire to chase statistics. “Morizo challenged us to create not simply a faster car,” says Naoyuki Sakamoto, its chief engineer, “but a car that gives the driver the confidence to keep pushing, even under the extreme conditions of the Nürburgring.” Learnings from the hydrogen-powered GR Corolla that competes in Japan’s endurance road racing series, Super Taikyu, extensively shaped the GRMN’s aerodynamic package, which includes a carbon-fiber hood with a unique center duct, new front side spoilers, carbon-fiber front fenders with unique ducts, and a rear wing with five settings.
The GRMN, along with 2025-and-newer GR Corollas, uses 45.6 more feet of structural adhesive for a stiffer body. Engine torque is up by 7 lb-ft, to 302, between 4000 and 4600 rpm. A GRMN-specific intercooler cooling system draws water from a gallon-sized tank in the rear, next to the battery, and sprays it on the intercooler for up to 150 seconds to reduce intake air temperature by 14 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit. The twin-tube shocks of the base GR-rolla have been swapped for monotube units, which are inverted at the front of the car. The GRMN is limited to 730 units globally (“primarily for North America, Japan, and Australia” per the release, priced at $65,655. The base car, for comparison, is $41,815.
Specs: 2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla
- Price: $65,655 (base)
- Powertrain: 1.6-liter turbocharged DOHC inline-three, six-speed manual
- Output: 300 hp at 6500 rpm, 302 lb-ft at 3250—4600 rpm
- Layout: All-wheel-drive, four-door, two-passenger subcompact hatchback
- Weight: 3218.7 pounds
- EPA Fuel Economy: 21/28/24mpg (city/hwy/combined)
- 0–60 mph: TBA
- Competition: Honda Civic Type R, Volkswagen Golf R
To see what this all adds up to, we spent some time behind the wheel and riding shotgun in the GRMN Corolla at Eagles Canyon Raceway near Decatur, Texas. The track is 2.7 miles long with 16 turns and 150 feet of elevation change. For this event, Toyota put a chicane in the back stretch and instructed us to pass through pit row every lap, decisions that limited the theoretical top speed per lap and helped keep the drivetrain cooler. All cars were set to Track Mode, which operates differently as of the 2025 model year: For the first two model years, Track Mode instructs the GR-Four system to split torque front/rear in a fixed, 50:50 ratio. For 2025 and newer cars, Track Mode is a variable mode that splits torque in different ratios (ranging from 60:40 to 30:70 front/rear) depending on driver inputs, the state of the vehicle, and the demands of the track.
To familiarize myself with the track, I hopped into an automatic-transmission, regular GR Corolla for a few laps. When I swapped into the GRMN, I immediately noticed a difference. The GRMN uses a much more aggressive tire—the street/track Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 vs. the Pilot Sport 4S summer—and the monotube shocks are much stiffer. I didn’t get to test how harsh the suspension/tire package is on the street, but on the track, they clarify feedback from the car significantly.
As I pushed the car harder and harder, under enthusiastic instruction from a pro in the right seat, I realized the car could handle much more power application than I thought it could, even when the wheels weren’t perfectly straight. Even as the tires started talking louder and louder, whether under acceleration or braking, the two Torsen LSDs and the clutched center driveline coupler shuffled power to help the car scramble out of every situation with its nose pointed in the right direction, the little three-cylinder snorting and snarling away. (According to Toyota, the system shifts from front- to rear-focused power at turn-in, maintains that rear bias through mid-corner, and at corner exit shifts power back toward the front.)
The AWD system gave me the confidence to push the car harder and experience more of what the car could do—in a rear-wheel-drive car, I would have had a lower comfort threshold. The GRMN forgave my mistakes, and rewarded me by gobbling up power gleefully when I fed it at the right moment, and nudging its blunt nose right or left under light throttle/brake inputs. The short wheelbase helped, too, by making rotation and understeer easier to detect than in a larger car. Both the brakes and the shifter were predictable and intuitive: The brake pedal is linear and never grabby, and the pleasantly clunky shifter is easy to operate without looking, thanks to notchy gates and fairly short throws.
For a car that represents an already sporty car refined by highly experienced drivers who are sensitive to every nuance, the GRMN is an absolute hoot to drive in the hands of a beginner. Your author is still a novice when it comes to track driving, but I had so much fun in this car—and I walked away a slightly better driver than I was before. The GRMN may be the most extreme GR Corolla yet, but like the other versions, it will put a smile on the faces of both beginners and advanced drivers alike. We’re glad this car exists.
2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla
Highs: Remarkably forgiving and fun on-track.
Lows: The hardest-core, limited-edition Corolla doesn’t come cheap. 
Summary: A spendy, track-day version of a special, smile-inducing car.

item.title: Scion’s Kei-01: Pocket-Sized Utility - Hagerty Media
item.text:
Media | Articles
Scion’s Kei-01: Pocket-Sized Utility
Stay up to speed with stories written by drivers, for drivers.
Get automotive news, DIY tips, market trends, in-depth car profiles, and more right in your email inbox.
Scion has chosen a thoroughly Japanese vehicle to usher in the brand’s revival in North America. The Kei-01 is essentially a rebadged model of Japan’s most popular kei truck, the Daihatsu Hijet (also sold as the Toyota Pixis), and it goes on sale, right-hand-drive and all, next year. Fleets get first dibs. Individuals? “Wait and see,” says Toyota. Price? We’ll have to get back to you on that. Patience may be the better part of valor here, because this is not America’s typical truck, and that is reason to both love it and approach it with clear expectations.
First off: If you’ve never driven a kei truck before (your author hadn’t), it really is fun. It looks like a toy from the outside, but once you swing open the short, light door and get settled behind the full-size steering wheel, it feels less foreign. Nothing inside the car is miniature. The HVAC switches, the plastic-handled shifter, the window switches: They’re all familiar. Materials-wise, everything is hard plastic or rubber, complemented by thin gray carpet and black cloth. Cheap? Yes. Charming in its simplicity? Absolutely. Trucks were born for utilitarian reasons, and in that sense the Kei-01 is purely traditional, down to its rubber mats and above-your-head shelf.
In our brief experience driving the Kei-01 on a short dirt-and-gravel loop, it reminded us of a shrunken Subaru. The ride was surprisingly comfortable: The four-wheel-drive truck pounded over the imperfect surface happily, without rattling our teeth. The accelerator pedal is touchy, and stabbing it provokes a surge of torque from the 660-cc three-cylinder that thrums under your butt. No, the engine is not at all powerful, but the vehicle it’s moving is light (likely around 2000 pounds), so it feels peppy at low speeds, even with a CVT. Compared to a UTV, it’s also fairly quiet. The brake pedal is light, and the feedback is minimal, though the little truck hauls down to a stop easily. Most Japanese-market Hijets use front discs and rear drums, though Toyota isn’t yet specifying the setup (or horsepower or torque) for the U.S.-market truck.
The steering feel and turning radius are the trucklet’s most striking aspects: At four turns lock-to-lock, maneuvering small spaces requires a lot of hand-over-hand action. Thankfully, the truck is very responsive. If you’ve never driven one before, you’ll be astounded at how it tucks its tiny little steel wheels under its body and chases its tail like a puppy. Not only can it maneuver in tight spaces, but it can also haul meaningful amounts of stuff into and through tight spaces thanks to a 600-pound payload and the ability to tow “small trailers.” (Again, Toyota’s keeping quiet on specs for now.) The hinged rear and sides of the dropside bed allow access to whatever you’re carrying. The bed doesn’t even rise to waist-height for an adult, so picking stuff out of it or putting stuff into it is easy.
The biggest difference between the U.S.-market Scion Kei-01 and its Daihatsu sibling (aside from the fact that the Scion will be built in Indiana) is the top speed. The only way Toyota can sell a right-hand-drive Japanese-market Daihatsu here without homologating the car is as a Low Speed Vehicle, as defined by the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), which govern all traits of all the vehicles sold here, down to the location of their turn signals. The LSV rules mandate a top speed of 25 mph. Installing a speed limiter is infinitely cheaper than designing a kei truck to meet the same crash standards as the “compact trucks” we know today. This Scion kei truck is a truly useful pickup, but its range of usefulness isn’t the same as the quarter- or half-tons we drive to work every day on the interstates at 75-plus. This tiny Scion was born for inner-city driving in Japan, and it’s coming to our shores practically unchanged—which is its allure and which also comes with real trade-offs.
So if you are tempted to be indignant that Toyota isn’t selling this straight to the public yet, perhaps consider whether it is the best vehicle for what you want it to do. We are used to vehicles that DO IT ALL, but as any classic car owner can tell you, it’s wise to know what your vehicle is built to do, and what it’s not built to do. Far from being limiting, understanding the limits of your vehicle frees you to enjoy it in the environments in which it excels.
Hagerty editor Stefan Lombard spent a summer driving a 4WD kei truck in such an environment—the cinder backroads of a national park in northern Arizona. “It was the perfect vehicle for puttering around on little patrols, checking up on cultural sites, hauling around signage and cleaning supplies, and generally exploring the woods,” he says. It was a capable little machine, too, he says, so naturally he tested it. “I discovered its limits while climbing a very steep, very rutted hill in 4-lo. Somewhere about three-quarters of the way up, it ran out of steam and I ran out of talent and then had to figure out how to get back down. There was one hairy moment where the thing began to teeter, so I just opened the door and planted my foot on the ground, which kept me upright. Never tried that again.”
Toyota’s fleet-only sales strategy for this Scion trucklet doesn’t mean you can’t own a kei truck in the U.S. You just can’t buy a new one. You can import a “classic” one (without a speed limiter, too) as long as it’s at least 25 years old. You may already live in a state that lets you title, register, and drive them on public roads, too: Last year, Colorado joined about 19 other states in legalizing kei trucks. Regulations differ greatly between states, so be sure to do your research before you start seriously shopping.
In our opinion, these are ideal vehicles for farms and ranches. We just wouldn’t take a Kei-01 into town. The drive would probably take forever, and besides, that’s what your full-size pickup is for!

Ford just released a new special-edition package for the Mustang GTD that pays homage to Henry Ford’s fabled race car, “Sweepstakes.” It’s called the Mustang GTD 1901, and it’s a tribute to a pivotal year in Ford’s history.
In 1901, Henry Ford was still just a struggling entrepreneur, hoping to make it big in the automotive industry. To garner some investor interest in what he had going on, he took his latest car, called “Sweepstakes,” and entered it in a car race in Grosse Pointe, Michigan. Ford ended up winning, investors took notice, and, well, 125 years later, the Mustang GTD has a striking new paint color.
The GTD 1901 will replace the Spirit of America package, which was a nod to Craig Breedlove, another man obsessed with speed and racing. For an undisclosed premium over the normal $325K-ish Mustang GTD, the 1901 gets a striking red and black exterior treatment. Ford calls the paint color Royal Red, and it looks sublime in these photos. Inside, there’s a matching Mahogany Red leather interior that gives this track missile an almost luxury-like feel.
Because the GTD 1901 is celebrating a race victory, Ford’s offering the Performance Package as standard on this version. The Performance Pack focuses on aerodynamic improvements, including a large splitter and dive planes up front, an active rear wing with a drag-reduction system, and underbody flaps to improve airflow.
Alongside this new package, the rest of the GTD lineup receives a handful of updates for the 2028 model year. The optional magnesium wheels, which shave roughly 50 lbs of unsprung weight over the standard aluminum wheels, are available in two new colors: Black or Luster Nickel. The 3D-printed paddle shifters and the shift ring on the eight-speed dual-clutch transmission have been redesigned. Inside, the cabin gets a bit ritzier with a full-grain leather wrap for the instrument panel, door panels, and center console. There are new painted stripe options for the exterior, and an updated color package for the GTD Liquid Carbon trim with flashy teal accents.
