item.title: Pernell Spohn Customs Creates One-Off Cars You Can Actually Use
item.text: Pernell Spohn doesn’t build custom cars because he wants to win trophies. His cars’ hand-formed metalwork and deftly integrated Corvette underpinnings won’t ever bask beneath the Autorama lights in pursuit of a Ridler . They certainly could , but for Spohn, that’s not the point. Spohn’s relationship with cars has not always been good, but it has been constant. “I was 25, 26 when I built this shop,” says Spohn of the neatly kept concrete block building located adjacent to his house in Butler, Pennsylvania. “I loved cars back when I was younger; then I started the shop and I hated cars,” he says. “I did a lot of frame work—I was the last-stop reconstruction shop—If I couldn’t fix it, they used it for parts.” Business was good; there were times he’d straighten the frames of three cars a day. That went on for decades, and while he had no shortage of customers, one day Spohn decided to make a pivot by restomodding a ’67 Firebird. One of Spohn’s frame-straightening rigs Rich Chenet That rekindled the flame. “After that, I was doing a car a year for myself, and after almost 10 years I had a collection of cars stacked up.” A local consignor talked Spohn into selling a half-dozen or so, and Spohn realized there might be a business in custom cars. Around that time, his sons decided to get involved, first Spencer and then his older son, Jonah. “It got to the point where I realized that my time is short and I needed to teach them my skills,” says Spohn. With that, the evolution from repair shop to one-off builds was complete. Pernell, Jonah, and Spencer Spohn Rich Chenet Calling anything Spohn has built after that ’67 Firebird a “restomod” would be an exponential understatement. He says of the ‘Bird: “I restomodded it, and I thought, ‘Man, this is going to be a really cool car.’ I drove [the finished car] around the block, which is a seven-mile journey, and I just shook my head. I couldn’t believe that when we were kids and we drove those cars, we had no idea that they were such a bucket of bolts.” That build was his motivation to go beyond the standard-issue restomod. Ever since, his builds deliver a fully modern driving experience. How does he do it? His secret, for cars, is the C6 Corvette chassis. Spohn has become an expert at grafting the frame and suspension of the ’05-13 Corvette under everything from a ’60 Buick to an E-Type Jag to, of all things, a Citroën Traction Avant. This is where Spohn’s years of working metal and frames come in handy—he’s completely undeterred by having to right-size the Corvette’s rails and then, subtly or not-so-subtly, massaging a metal body around it. Rich Chenet Rich Chenet Rich Chenet We walk up to a deep purple ’60 Buick Invicta. “That one has a 2010 Grand Sport under it. The Buick was about 22 inches longer, so we had to lengthen the frame and the torque tube.” He doesn’t stop at getting the wheelbase lined up and bolting the body down—that’d be too easy. “The entire floor pan, tunnel, firewall, everything had to be made. Basically, this has a Corvette frame that was bared and lengthened, and then I unitized the body to the frame. I create a unibody for every car because of the strength—there’s no flex.” Even the inner fenders and radiator support are now structural. Rich Chenet Rich Chenet Next to the Buick sit three more of his builds. Imagine how your 8-year-old self—or a veteran Hot Wheels designer—would have sculpted the ideal Chevy C10, ’68 Camaro, or Jag E-Type, and you won’t be far off from Spohn’s creations. Rich Chenet Rich Chenet Rich Chenet “That Camaro is 13 inches wider than stock in the back, and 12 inches wider up front,” Spohn says, pointing to the 355 section-width tires that sit just barely inside the rear fenders. “Low and wide, that’s what makes them handle. So everything goes wide,” he says. Under the rear wheel well of the bright-sky blue, two-seat Camaro, where you’d typically feel the sharp edge of the panel, or the rolled-flat lip of doubled-over sheetmetal, rests what feels like small-diameter pipe. “On my cars I put 3/8ths stainless-steel tubing around the lip of the wheel well. That way if it hits it’s not going to deform the fender. And they do occasionally hit—I get after it pretty hard in that car.” Rich Chenet We move on to the searingly yellow pickup. It’s immediately recognizable as a C10, but there isn’t a single body panel that Spohn hasn’t massaged. Beneath this, and all the trucks Spohn builds, is the chassis of a late-model GM truck. “We also use the firewall and the floor out of the new truck because that’s where all your main components attach: Your brakes, HVAC, everything that’s got all the engineering in it all bolts right back up. The seats actually bolt in, too.” He then blends the old cab and cowl to fit around the modern hard points. Rich Chenet Rich Chenet As wild as he’s willing to get with a vehicle’s body, Spohn relies on the original manufacturer when he can for the mechanical bits. “OEM parts have so much engineering behind them,” he says. “If I can make an OEM product work in a build, I know it’s going to work for a long time.” Along that vein, and because it was intended as a shop vehicle for their business, Spohn didn’t go nuts with the C10’s drivetrain. “We kept the five-three in it and added an LT4 supercharger, and it makes 480 lb-ft to the wheels. We could’ve spent more on it, but it’s plenty for what it is.” The added benefit of his OEM-first approach is that everything continues to run through the factory body control module, which eliminates a massive layer of complexity. No matter how fancy they may look on the outside, Spohn’s builds operate like the modern vehicles they effectively are. Rich Chenet He’s arrived at this approach through a lot of trial and error, and it’s clear Spohn doesn’t stop iterating until something meets his expectations or the vision he has for the project. Once something works, he sticks with it, but Spohn isn’t one for shortcuts. That was apparent from the moment I set foot in his shop, and it’s perhaps no more evident than with his ’69 E-Type. Rich Chenet The car had been someone’s project, a hardtop made into a convertible at some point years ago, so Spohn didn’t feel bad about pulling it apart. He ended up making the whole body himself, even the windshield surround, from 20-gauge steel and aluminum. Spohn in the early phases of working on the Jag’s hood. Rich Chenet Rich Chenet Rich Chenet Rich Chenet “I have so much time in this. This hood is from an original piece—on the factory cars, the whole front end tilted up in one piece,” he shares as he points to the hood cut lines he made, which come in above the headlights. “My biggest mistake was making it split over the top of the light and go the whole way to the front,” he adds wistfully. “If I had made the front end one piece, it would’ve saved me probably three weeks.” That said, it’s probably structurally stiffer this way, and he made it work as if it were OEM, custom-fabricated hinges and all. It’s hard to improve upon the beauty and simplicity of an E-Type; Spohn’s creation instead adds the voluptuousness you’d find in a TVR or a Viper or a Cobra to yield a very aggressive and handsome roadster that has a look all its own. I caught it just in time—its new owner was set to pick it up the following day. “This was a big challenge, particularly because of the radiator,” says Spohn, noting how tough it is to squeeze the chonk of a modern three-quarter-ton diesel truck within the confines of a comparably svelte, minimally modified Square-Body. item.title: New York Just Banned Subscriptions For Features Your Car Already Has
item.text:
New York Just Banned Subscriptions For Features Your Car Already Has
In-vehicle subscriptions are pretty universally maligned among car owners. Most folks don't like the feeling of having to pay every month for features their cars were supposed to come with, and now New York State is doing something about it. Governor Kathy Hochul just signed a bill that bars automakers, dealers and their agents from selling subscriptions for features that are already installed.
The new law, which takes effect on February 27, 2027, is part of a new section of the state's General Business Law, according to Spectrum News. You can read the law for yourself here. It lays out fairly simple ground rules when it comes to subscriptions dealers or manufacturers can offer you: The feature must use hardware already in the car when it was bought or leased, and it must keep working without continual costs or support from the automaker or a third party. Those two things pretty much bring an end to crap like subscription-based heated seats and alike. It also is supposed to cover hands-off driving systems and enhanced navigation. Basically, once the hardware is physically in the car and the manufacturer isn't paying anything for you to use it, they can't then charge you. OEMs will also not be able to charge for software updates that fix safety defects.
Hochul called the practice a "deceptive business model," according to CBS 6 Albany. She also told automakers to keep their hands out of New Yorkers' wallets. It passed through the New York State Senate 57-3.
Some caveats
As with all good things, there are some exceptions. First of all, your lease or payment plan doesn't count as a subscription, so don't even try it, slick.
The law also doesn't apply to navigation updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle WiFi, telematics, roadside assistance or "vehicle-connected services" that rely on cellular data or other networks, according to Motor1. It also exempts software-dependent driver assistance features, like Tesla's Full Self-Driving or GM's Super Cruise.
I know what you're thinking. Didn't I just mention that hands-free driving systems are covered? Well, yes, but subscriptions tied to software and data are likely to survive, while hardware-only features are the real targets. Automakers will almost certainly make the argument that things like FSD and Super Cruise are "connected" or "software-dependent."
One prime example of what this bill aims to get rid of is BMW keeping things like a 360-degree camera behind a paywall. That hardware is already built into the car, and, as we reported, it doesn't require a data connection to operate. It's the same thing with features like high-beam assist and remote start, so I imagine it'll be hard for BMW and other companies with similar schemes to argue that these are "connected." I mean, these are the same people who argue that buyers actually want subscriptions, which is certainly not true.
In any case, violators will face civil penalties of up to $250 per point-of-sale for each violation, though it's not clear exactly how that'll be counted. It's not clear if other states are going to follow suit, but here's hoping.

item.text:
Genesis Targets 640 Miles With EREV SUV That Could Beat Scout To Market
As pure EV demand cools, Genesis is betting on gas-assisted extended-range luxury EVs to help eliminate charger worries and range anxiety.
Two factors have slowed the popularity of electric vehicles among U.S. buyers: charging and range. Genesis hopes to end both of those concerns starting with a new extended-range EV (EREV) that, if it stays on track, will beat Scout Motors to market. Hyundai's latest product roadmap places this new Genesis EREV SUV firmly in the first half of 2027, and the automaker teased some of the details about this vehicle during a roundtable discussion at the LA Auto Show that CarScoops was a part of.
There are plenty of unanswered questions about what it'll be, what it'll look like, and how much it'll cost, but one thing is clear, Genesis is aiming for a total driving range of 640 miles. While we wait for a firm U.S. delivery date, Ash Corson, product planning boss at Genesis gave us some info to stew on. Let's take a look at what we do know about the EREV that could launch well before Scout gets on the road.
What we know
Both Genesis and Hyundai are planning EREV launches in early 2027. For Hyundai, we know that'll come in the form of the Santa Fe, and it will be part of the company's plant expansion in Alabama. Genesis hasn't revealed the name of its upcoming EREV but did tease it with the photo above. There's no way to be completely certain, but that sure looks like the GV70 to us. The brand made clear in the past that it was open to possibly pursuing a GV90 EREV, but we expect it to launch next year as an EV only. Importantly, Genesis mentioned a D-segment SUV as an EREV product, which could be GV70 or GV80.
Hyundai has openly said that its EREV platform will use less than half the battery capacity of a comparable EV. Despite that smaller pack size, it's targeting more than 640 miles of total range. The brand says it'll pull that off thanks in part to new in-house-developed battery cells that can evidently provide all the output necessary to match the performance of comparable EVs.
According to Corson, the benefits of an EREV make it more accessible to people who want an EV but don't necessarily have the home charging access or short daily commutes that traditional battery-electric vehicles more practical. "Some people have a garage, and it's great because they can charge an EV there. It's a wonderful experience," he said, and added. "A lot of people don't. Some people live in more rural areas where you have longer distances between refueling, whether that's charging or gas. So, I think providing the customer a choice of what powertrain makes sense for them is really key."
What's an EREV?
The basic platform here is very straightforward. An extended-range EV is an EV at heart. Owners can charge it like any other EV, whether that's at home or at a public charging station. The distinction is that an EREV platform also incorporates a gas-burning engine that kicks on to, you guessed it, extend the vehicle's range. Its sole job is to charge the battery, so the gas engine doesn't actually drive the wheels — it's basically an on-board generator.
That's key because it effectively ends the concern of charging station availability and charging speed. For those who can charge conveniently at home or work or elsewhere, they can run around with zero fuel in the tank and run in pure EV mode all the time. For those who might not have that ability, they can fill the gas tank and know that it'll charge the battery as they're driving. Both groups also benefit because long road trips become no big deal since a quick fuel stop is all they need to keep going.

item.title: Slate Thinks 205 Miles Is More Than Enough Range
item.text:
Slate Thinks 205 Miles Is More Than Enough Range
Slate Auto is in a strange spot. Yes, with a starting price of $26,400, including destination, the two-door pickup truck it's selling is cheap compared to the competition, but it also lacks basic features like power windows and a radio at that price. With options that'll make the truck more livable for everyday use, prices will quickly climb. No matter which options they choose, they'll still be saddled with the same 205 miles of range. Even though that's quite meager by today's standards, Slate feels that's more than enough to win over customers.
It makes sense why the Slate has such a shoddy range, even compared to its competition. The battery is the single most expensive part of an electric vehicle, so an automaker looking to make a cheap EV will use a smaller battery. There's a view that Slate's approach could work for folks who are already comfortable with EVs, but it might not translate for those more accustomed to what gas-powered vehicles offer, according to Automotive News. There's also the issue that similarly priced rivals will offer more range on base models, and they usually have the option of extended-range batteries.
Still, Slate feels 205 miles is really all the average American needs from a vehicle like its truck, the cheapest EV and pickup for sale in the U.S. To be fair, it's also the smallest pickup in the U.S. — about two feet shorter than a Ford Maverick. In a marketing email sent earlier this month, Slate said 205 miles is "more than [many people] need each day." That's sort of fair, because according to a 2024 survey done by AAA, the average American drives about 31 miles per day, meaning that from full to empty, you'd only need to charge the Slate about once a week. Of course, no one actually drives like that, and the range will never actually be 205 miles, but we can't really account for that.
The competition
Slate isn't the only company offering an EV with less-than-stellar range. The Kia EV3 compact crossover, which starts at $31,385, comes as standard with 221 miles of range. While the starting prices are far different, the EV3 comes with a lot more from the get-go. To get the Slate to a comparable place, you've got to add a bed kit that brings in seats and a roof — giving the Slate "crossover" a $31,400 base price, according to AutoNews. It'll still be missing plenty of other things at that price, like a radio and electric windows.
In any case, Kia doesn't expect this low-range EV3 to be a big seller — capturing just 3 to 5% of its sales. The higher Wind trim, with its 321 miles of range and $36,485 starting price, is expected to be the volume seller with about 60% of sales. That sort of speaks to Slate's problem. It seems like folks would rather pay the extra money to not have to worry about range anxiety or charging up their cars as often.
In reality, the EV3 isn't a direct competitor to the Slate, but Ford's yet-to-be-unveiled Fathom pickup is. It's expected to have a standard battery with around 250 miles of range and an optional battery with over 300 miles, Automotive News reports. Despite the fact it range-mogs the Slate, its starting price will come in at $29,945, including shipping, and it'll be an actual vehicle with the sort of modern luxuries and conveniences you'd expect in today's day and age.
I'm not saying that the Slate is dead on arrival by any means, but I do think the Jeff Bezos-backed company is really, really hoping that there are a lot of Quirked Up Individuals out there who will fall for the proletariat virtual signals of crank windows, no radio, a key you've got to insert and no screen while also paying a price that doesn't really connect with that reality. I'm not sure they're out there.

item.title: Ineos To Build The Grenadier In The US
item.text:
Ineos To Build The Grenadier In The US
If it materializes, Ineos' plan could cash in on surging American demand while sidestepping steep import tariffs.
America went years without being able to buy a Defender. Now it might end up building two totally different versions of it — although only one of them is officially sanctioned – that are made in the U.S. First JLR said it planned to build Defender-branded vehicles in the U.S. with Stellantis, and now U.K.-based Ineos, whose Grenadier was inspired by the original Defender, is also looking to set up production across the pond.
Ineos Automotive announced that it wants to start building both the Grenadier SUV and Quartermaster pickup brother in the U.S. in 2028. It claims to have already shortlisted some sites and expects to name the winner in the next few months. Given the short timeframe, these are obviously pre-existing plants. Ineos currently builds its truck and SUV at an old Smart plant in Hambach, France.
The brand was created by petrochemical billionaire Jim Ratcliffe after JLR decided to axe the Defender in 2016, and Ratcliffe wanted something in the same vein. Like the old Defender, and unlike the new unibody one, the Grenadier is a tough body-on-frame truck with recirculating ball steering, solid axles and lockable diffs.
Ineos in the U.S.
A massive 70% of Grenadier sales come from U.S. buyers, which could be significant enough to consider moving American production to North America. But throw in the impact of President Trump's tariffs, and it becomes almost essential. It's why JLR has inked a deal with Stellantis, and why Audi last month announced a $4 billion investment to build a plant in Georgia.
Hopefully, building the Grenadier and Quartermaster in the U.S. might allow Ineos to bring its prices down, although it hasn't promised anything of the sort. The MY27 SUV starts at $73,745 including destination, and the pickup has an $86,390 entry point. That makes both Ineos models more expensive than comparable offerings from Ford, GM, and Toyota.
All U.S.-spec Grenadiers and Quartermasters come with a turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-6 from BMW that makes 282 horsepower (285 PS) and 332 pound-feet (450 Nm) of torque. European buyers also get the option of a second 3.0-liter inline-6 BMW engine, this one a 245 hp diesel. Both types send their power to all four wheels though an eight-speed automatic transmission and return pretty awful 14-15 mpg fuel economy.

Celebrity Chef Gordon Ramsay Set To Host New 'Top Gear' Episodes
What will be the first car called an 'Idiot Sandwich?'
The BBC is cooking up a new series of Top Gear, and celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay is heading the presenter lineup. Filming starts in 2027, the BBC says, but the first of the new shows won't air until 2028. Which gives the production team plenty of time to get the on-site catering up to scratch at the Top Gear Test Track. Something tells us Ramsey isn't going to be happy settling on a soggy sausage roll for lunch.
The Stig returns to offer Ramsay some silent but important on-screen backup, though there's no word yet on who the other presenters might be. But the BBC promises "epic adventures, daring tests and spectacular stunts," so it sounds like the central premise of the show won't change, even if the bodies in front of the camera are new.
Ramsay isn't technically new to Top Gear at all, having appeared as a guest three times already, starting with the first series of the reinvented Jeremy Clarkson-led lineup in 2002, and most recently, in 2017. His best lap of the Top Gear track was 1 minute 46.3 seconds at the wheel of a Chevrolet Lacetti, which was enough to secure him seventh place on the show's 'A Star In A Reasonably Priced Car' leaderboard.
The fiery-tempered, cuss-lovin' 60-year-old chef made his name in the culinary world before achieving even greater fame on TV with shows like 'Hell's Kitchen.' But Ramsay is also well known for his collection of exotica that currently includes a Ferrari F40.
"My love affair with cars began as a child, growing up a field away from Silverstone, where I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing," Ramsay said. "[This is] an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can't wait to get started!"
Morgan crash killed TG's last incarnation
Top Gear started in the 1970s, but didn't become the cultural behemoth it is today until 2002. That's when former presenter Jeremy Clarkson was lured back with the promise of free rein to create a totally new kind of car show where boring was banned.
The golden era lasted until 2015, when Clarkson punched a producer off-screen and was fired. Clarkson and fellow presenters Richard Hammond and James May went on to repeat their act on an even bigger scale for Amazon's The Grand Tour, but that wasn't the end of Top Gear. The BBC rebooted the show in 2016, and after more presenter changes, it appeared to have found its groove again with motoring journalist Chris Harris, former cricketer Freddie Flintoff, and comedian Paddy McGuinness at the helm.
But the wheels came off when Flintoff was horrifically injured while driving a Morgan 3 Wheeler at the test track in 2022. The Morgan flipped over, and Flintoff was dragged along the ground for 160 ft (50 m), leaving him with permanent facial scars. The show was axed, and Flintoff later reached a confidential settlement with the BBC believed to be worth £9 million ($12 m).
Top Gear refused to stay dead, though. Plans to revive the UK version one more time were confirmed in August 2026.
"This won't be a nostalgic reboot," Suzy Lamb, Managing Director, BBC Studios Entertainment, said, adding that Ramsay's "passion, mischief [and] competitive streak" make him a perfect fit for the lead role.

Audi Is Bringing Back The RS 6 Sedan To Fight The BMW M5
The next Audi RS 6 was caught attacking the Nürburgring in sedan form with flared fenders, oval tailpipes and an electrified powertrain.
Audi is almost ready to unveil the next generation of the RS 6, crowning the new A6 lineup. The new performance model is expected to be fitted with an electrified powertrain, targeting the plug-in hybrid BMW M5. Furthermore, unlike its wagon-only predecessor, the new Audi RS 6 will also be available in a sedan body style, breaking a 15-year-old tradition.
Our spy photographers caught a camouflaged prototype of the upcoming Audi RS 6 sedan doing hot laps at the Nürburgring. The model looks more production-ready compared to a similar prototype spotted exactly one year ago, as it rides on different alloy wheels and comes fitted with the final oval tailpipes. This suggests that development is close to completion ahead of an expected global launch in 2027.
The Audi RS6 will wear sportier bumpers in combination with wider front and rear fenders. The greatest indication we have is the wide-bodied A6 Allroad, although the RS 6 will swap plastic cladding and skid plates for splitters and side skirts. The sedan appears to have a subtle lip spoiler at the back, while retaining the full-width LED taillights of the regular A6.
More power thanks to electrification
The yellow high-voltage warning sticker on the windshield of the prototype confirms that the next-gen Audi RS6 will transition into an electrified powertrain. What remains unclear is the cylinder count of the internal combustion engine.
A potential candidate is an uprated version of the twin-turbo 2.9-liter V6 plug-in hybrid setup which is good for a combined 630 horsepower in the smaller RS 5. Another option is the high-performance twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 plug-in hybrid used by Porsche and Bentley, which makes 771 hp in the Continental GT.
Either way, the output is expected to rival the 717 hp plug-in hybrid V8 of the BMW M5 which is about to receive a Neue Klasse facelift. This means that the newcomer will be significantly more powerful than the outgoing RS 6 Avant GT which makes 621 hp from a mild-hybrid V8.
Audi Sport boss Rolf Michl spoke to Australian outlet CarSales earlier this year, revealing that the next RS 6 needs to "tow horses, yachts, boats". He also added it will retain the character of a "luxurious travel machine", combining performance and sovereignty.
The last time Audi offered an RS 6 sedan was in the V10-powered C6 generation that bowed out in 2011, followed by the Avant-only C7 and C8 models. The C9 generation is expected to break cover over the next few months, ahead of a market launch next year.

item.title: Why This Guards Red 2004 Porsche Carrera GT Could Fetch $6.5 Million
item.text:
Why This Guards Red 2004 Porsche Carrera GT Could Fetch $6.5 Million
The rare paint color and pampered history could help this car fetch nearly 17 times its original sticker price
They don't make them like they used to. This classic aphorism appears especially relevant to the current state of the supercar and hypercar market, where cars from the 1990s and early 2000s are now starting to sell for previously inconceivable figures. Case in point: a red 2004 Porsche Carrera GT that's expected to sell for between $5.5 million and $6.5 million next month.
As recently as a couple of years ago, it was possible to buy a pristine Carrera GT for less than $1.5 million in the U.S. Prices have since surged, and this year alone, several Carrera GTs have each sold at auction for over $3 million, and in March, one sold for $6.7 million. If this red car reaches the pre-auction estimate, it'll be one of the priciest Carrera GTs ever sold.
The highlight is the color. This is one of just 80 examples painted in Guards Red (only 42 of which were U.S.-spec models), which makes it the rarest standard factory color, according to RM Sotheby's. Only 1,270 Carrera GTs were produced from 2003 through 2006, and the auction listing indicates this car lived a pampered life with just 2,203 miles on the odometer.
A recent service cost almost $90,000
The Porsche Carrera GT is regarded as one of the last analog supercars, so maintaining and preserving one isn't cheap – shown by a recent service receipt for this car. Earlier this year, the car was sent to Graham Rahal Performance in Indiana and underwent a full service for a cool $88,056. The service saw the original radio replaced by an updated one with Bluetooth functionality, a new Öhlins suspension system was fitted, and the exhaust was modified. The owner also paid a staggering $24,249 for an official Carrera GT dark gray luggage set.
Then there's the cost of maintaining the powertrain itself. A full engine service cost $46,601, including $7,200 worth of labor. As part of the service, the ignition coils, air filters, two intake camshafts, the spark plugs, the thermostat, and a host of O-rings and bolts were replaced. The car also got fresh 0W40 Mobil 1 Supercar synthetic engine oil, new coolant, and new gear oil.
The most legendary aspect of the Carrera GT is its engine. It's the only Porsche road car that used a V10 engine, with the screaming naturally aspirated 5.7-liter unit delivering 603 horsepower at 8,000 rpm and 435 pound-feet of torque at 5,750 rpm. This engine is mated exclusively to a six-speed manual transmission driving the rear wheels. When it was new, it cost about $390,000 in the U.S. if the auction estimate is correct, this car could sell for roughly 17 times that figure.

item.angle: R32 era and the Godzilla nickname
item.text:
The Nissan Skyline GT-R (Japanese: 日産・スカイラインGT-R, Hepburn: Nissan Sukairain GT-R) is a Japanese grand tourer based on the Nissan Skyline range. The first cars named "Skyline GT-R" were produced between 1969 and 1972 under the model code KPGC10, and were successful in Japanese touring car racing events. This model was followed by a brief production run of second-generation cars, under model code KPGC110, in 1973.
After a 16-year hiatus, the GT-R name was revived in 1989 as the BNR32 ("R32") Skyline GT-R. Group A specification versions of the R32 GT-R were used to win the Japanese Touring Car Championship for four years in a row. The R32 GT-R also had success in the Australian Touring Car Championship, with Jim Richards using it to win the championship in 1991 and Mark Skaife doing the same in 1992, until a regulation change excluded the GT-R in 1993. The technology and performance of the R32 GT-R prompted the Australian motoring publication Wheels to nickname the GT-R "Godzilla" in its July 1989 edition. Wheels then carried the name through all the generations of Skyline GT-Rs, most notably the R34 GT-R, which they nicknamed "Godzilla Returns", and described as "The best handling car we have ever driven". In tests conducted by automotive publications, the R34 GT-R covered a quarter of a mile  (402 metres) in 12.2 seconds from a standing start time and accelerated from 0–100 km/h (0–62 mph) in 4.4 seconds.
The Skyline GT-R became the flagship of Nissan performance, showing many advanced technologies including the ATTESA E-TS all-wheel drive system and the Super-HICAS four-wheel steering. Today, the car is popular for import drag racing, circuit track, time attack and events hosted by tuning magazines. Production of the Skyline GT-R ended in August 2002. The car was replaced by the GT-R (R35), an all-new vehicle based on an enhanced version of the Skyline V36 platform. Although visibly different, the two vehicles share similar design features and are manufactured in the same factory.
The Skyline GT-R was never manufactured outside Japan, and the sole export markets were Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia and New Zealand, in 1991, and the UK (in 1997, due to the Single Vehicle Approval scheme). They are also popular across the world as used Japanese imports.
The Skyline GT-R has become an iconic sports car as a grey import in the Western world (mainly the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland, Canada, and the United States). It has become notable through pop culture such as The Fast and the Furious, Initial D, Shakotan Boogie, Tokyo Xtreme Racer, Wangan Midnight, Need for Speed, Forza, Driving Emotion Type-S, Test Drive, and Gran Turismo.
In 2019, Nismo announced that it would resume production of spare parts for all generations of the Skyline GT-R, including body panels and engines.


== History of the brand ==

The Skyline name originated from Prince automobile company, which developed and sold the Skyline line of sedans before merging with Nissan-Datsun.
The original Skyline was launched by the Prince Motor Company in April 1957 and was powered by a 1.5-litre engine. The later iteration launched in 1964 called the Prince Skyline GT was powered by a 2.0-litre G7 inline-6 engine shared with the up market Prince Gloria sedan. Two road going versions were built. The S54A which had a single carburettor engine rated at 78 kW (106 PS; 105 hp) and the S54B which had a triple carburettor engine rated at 92 kW (125 PS; 123 hp) and production totalled 100 units.

The GT-R abbreviation stands for Gran Turismo–Racing while the GT-B stands for Gran Turismo–Berlinetta. The Japanese chose to use Italian naming conventions when naming the car – as most cars that were made in Japan at that time used Western abbreviations – to further enhance sales. The earliest predecessor of the GT-R, the S54 2000 GT-B, came second in its first race in the 1964 Japanese GP to the purpose-built Porsche 904 GTS. However, the earlier Prince Skyline Sport coupé/convertible foreshadowed the GT-R as the first sports-oriented model in the Skyline range, hence the name.
The next development of the GT-R, the four-door PGC10 2000 GT-R, scored 33 victories in the one and a half years it raced, and by the time it attempted its 50th consecutive win, its run was ended by a Mazda Savanna RX-3. The car took 1,000 victories by the time it was discontinued in 1972. The last of the original GT-R models, the KPGC110 2000GT-R, used an unchanged S20 119 kW (160 hp) inline-6 engine from the earlier 2000 GT-R and only 197 units were sold due to the worldwide energy crisis. This model was the only GT-R to never participate in a major race despite being developed as a sole purpose-built race car, which now resides in Nissan's storage unit for historical cars in Zama.
The Skyline continued into the 1990s when it became popular largely because it remained rear wheel drive, while most other manufacturers were focusing on front wheel drive cars.
Throughout its lifetime, various special editions containing additional performance-enhancing modifications were introduced by Nissan and its performance division Nismo (Nissan Motorsport).


== First generation (C10; 1969–1972) ==

The first Skyline GT-R, known by the internal Nissan designation of PGC10, was introduced on 4 February 1969, and was exclusive to Japanese Nissan dealership network called Nissan Prince Store when the Prince company was integrated into Nissan operations in 1966. It was available originally as a four-door sedan after a public debut at the October 1968 Tokyo Motor Show as the Skyline 2000GT. It was advertised alongside the R380 racecar to showcase the Skyline's racing heritage. It was equipped with the 2.0 L DOHC S20 Inline-six engine rated at 119 kW (162 PS; 160 hp) at 7,000 rpm and 176 N⋅m (130 lb⋅ft) at 5,600 rpm. Power was delivered to the rear wheels by a 5-speed manual transmission and the car was equipped with a limited-slip differential. The first Skyline GT-R rode on a semi-trailing arm strut suspension. The braking system consisted of disc brakes at the front and drum brakes at the rear.
In October 1970, a minor change to the base Skyline introduced a two-door coupé bodystyle with the chassis code KPGC10. Aside from the changes made to the C10 series as a whole, the only changes specific to the KPGC10 model from the PGC10 included the addition of black FRP overbumpers to the rear wheel arches, a change from bullet-shaped to Talbot- shaped wing mirrors, and a redesigned front grille.
The interior of the car was very basic and featured racing bucket seats and a three-spoke steering wheel along with wood inserts. The pedals were finished in aluminium.
A popular name for the PGC and KPGC10 Skyline GT-R was Hakosuka, which combines the Japanese word for box ("hako" or ハコ) and the pronounced abbreviation of skyline ("Suka" or スカ as in スカイライン or "sukairain").
A total of 832 PGC10 and 1,197 KPGC10 Skyline GT-Rs were produced.

item.title: You Want the Full-On, Raw-and-Racy Sports Car Experience? This Lotus Emira is It
item.text:
Overview
There are few cars on the market today that scratch the same itch as the 2027 Lotus Emira. This lightweight, purpose-built sports car feels like something out of the history books, a celebration of the analog-style driving that car enthusiasts yearn for from the good ol' days. A turbocharged four-cylinder or naturally aspirated V-6 sits midship behind a two-seat cabin; a six-speed manual is available, although only with the V-6. Driving the Emira is a racy, full-immersion experience.
As good as the Emira is to drive, it's a sports car from a small, boutique automaker, and therefore, it comes with compromises. For one, its six-figure price tag doesn't buy the same level of luxury or fit and finish as rivals such as the Chevrolet Corvette or the Maserati GranTurismo. But that's always been what Lotus cars delivered to the driver, and that's why the Emira is something to be savored.
Expert Tip: Speaking of sports cars from the past, Lotus is in the process of developing a new range-topping supercar with a V-8 hybrid powertrain. We think it will revive the legendary Esprit nameplate and might be worth waiting for.
What's New for 2027?
A slightly more powerful 420 Sport trim joins the lineup this year, with 14 more horsepower than the standard Turbo SE model. The 420 Sport can be had with an optional Lightweight Handling package, which is said to reduce curb weight by 55 pounds by replacing the Emira's exhaust system with a new titanium one and swapping some other parts for carbon fiber alternatives. The package also includes aerodynamic tweaks to improve downforce and boost airflow to the Emira's radiators, as well as new two-way adjustable dampers from Multimatic. Elsewhere in the lineup, a new removable glass roof panel has been added as an option to all trims.
If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
Compare the 2027 Lotus Emira to other vehicles you're interested in
Our new comparison tool provides a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of up to five vehicles of your choice.
Engine, Transmission, and Performance
- Engines: 400-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder, 414-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder, 400-hp supercharged 3.5-liter V-6
- Transmissions: 6-speed automatic, 8-speed dual-clutch automatic, 6-speed manual
- Drivetrain: rear-wheel drive
The mid-engine Emira can be had with either of two powerplants. A turbocharged four-cylinder sourced from Mercedes-AMG is standard and makes 400 horsepower in the SE trims and 414 horsepower in the 420 Sport trim. It feeds the rear wheels through an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission, the only gearbox pairing with the turbo-four. A Toyota-sourced supercharged 3.5-liter V-6 is optional. It also makes 400 horsepower, but it works through either a six-speed torque-converter automatic or a six-speed manual transmission.
Unlike most other modern sports cars, the Emira forgoes electric power steering for a hydraulically assisted setup that provides unsurpassed feel and feedback. During our initial test drive, we praised the Emira's balanced handling and brilliant steering, and we marveled at its commitment to driver involvement. The Emira is not without its quirks; the manual transmission's lever action requires a deliberate push to swap gears swiftly, and the brakes are grabby and difficult to modulate smoothly. We also drove the 420 Sport and enjoyed its quick-shifting dual-clutch transmission, extra power, and natural handling.
What's Your Car Worth?
Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.
0–60-MPH Times
- C/D 60-mph Test: 4.3 seconds (V-6 Manual), 3.4 seconds (2.0T Automatic)
In Comparison: At our test track, an Emira with the V-6 and manual transmission hit 60 mph in 4.3 seconds and completed the quarter-mile run in 12.7 seconds at 111 mph. The Lotus beat the Nissan Z Performance manual, which needed 4.5 seconds to hit 60 mph and 13.0 seconds to complete the quarter-mile. The Z, however, costs less than half the Emira, but it's the Lotus's intense driving experience you're paying for rather than blazing speed. The Emira's turbocharged four-cylinder proved quicker in our testing, running to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPG
- EPA City Ratings: 16-18 mpg
- EPA Highway Ratings: 24-26 mpg
The EPA estimates fuel economy for the Emira as high as 18 mpg city, 26 mpg highway, and 21 mpg combined. With the manual transmission, the V-6 model earned estimates of 16 mpg city, 24 mpg highway, and 19 mpg combined. For more information about the Emira's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
First Row: With a simple design and seating for two, the Emira's interior is both minimalistic and intimate. The driver faces a squared-off steering wheel and a 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster. The material quality looks upscale, and there is physical switchgear for the climate controls. As is Lotus's wont, the Emira fulfills the role of a stripped-back sports car, with most modern frivolities checked at the door. But there are some practical touches inside, including cupholders in the center console and storage bins in the doors that can each allegedly accommodate a half-liter bottle.
Cargo Capacity: There is a seven-cubic-foot cargo space behind the seats and another five cubic feet available in a storage bay behind the engine. However, we'd caution you against using the rearmost cargo space for anything that's temperature sensitive due to its proximity to the Emira's powertrain and exhaust components.
Infotainment and Connectivity
- Infotainment: 10.2-inch touchscreen
- Connectivity: Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto
- Audio System: 7-speaker stereo (standard), 11-speaker KEF stereo (optional)
The Emira's infotainment system runs through a 10.2-inch touchscreen mounted in the middle of the dashboard. Apart from controls on the steering wheel, there is a knob on the center console to adjust volume and play or pause audio; otherwise, there are no physical controls for the infotainment system.
Along with 12-volt and USB charging ports, the Emira features standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto smartphone functionality, both of which work wirelessly. A seven-speaker stereo is standard, but the 11-speaker KEF premium stereo setup is worth the upgrade.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
Breaking with Lotus tradition, the Emira is offered with a host of driver-assistance technology, but the good stuff—including adaptive cruise control—is optional.
- Standard Safety Features: automated emergency braking, blind-spot monitoring, front and rear parking sensors
- Optional Safety Features: adaptive cruise control, rear cross-traffic alert, automatic high-beam headlamps

item.title: Lotus Eletre X Launches in UAE With 938 hp and 1,200 km Hybrid Range - ArabWheels
item.text:
AGMC launched the Lotus Eletre X in the UAE on November 24, 2026, with prices starting at AED 299,900. The new plug-in hybrid SUV delivers up to 938 hp (700 kW), while Lotus claims a combined range of up to 1,200 km.
Its onboard petrol-powered generator reduces reliance on public charging during longer journeys between emirates. The hybrid model joins the existing all-electric Eletre in Lotus’s UAE lineup. Lotus offers two variants locally: the Eletre X Hybrid and the more powerful Eletre X Hybrid SE. With an entry price of AED 299,900, the hybrid offers a more affordable entry point into Lotus’s SUV range.
According to Lotus, the Eletre X weighs up to 120 kg less than the all-electric Eletre 900. Engineers achieved these savings by changing the body structure, electric drive system, and battery base plate. The reduced weight aims to improve handling without compromising the SUV’s everyday practicality.
Exterior Design and Cabin Upgrades
The Lotus Eletre X measures 5,103 mm in length and has a 3,019 mm wheelbase, retaining the proportions of the all-electric Eletre. The standard exterior kit includes soft-close doors, a high-gloss black rear badge, and an integrated floating roof spoiler.
According to Lotus, the active rear spoiler can generate up to 120 kg of downforce under heavy braking. A panoramic glass roof with PDLC electronic dimming allows occupants to adjust light transmission into the cabin.
The 5-seat cabin features carbon fiber decorative inlays and a sport alloy accelerator pedal. Listed equipment includes a 15.1” mini-LED touchscreen and a 23-speaker KEF Reference Audio system. The Comfort Seat Pack includes front-seat massage, adjustable bolsters, cushion extensions, rear-seat heating, and ventilation for both seating rows.
X Hybrid Powertrain and Performance
The Lotus Eletre X uses a series-type plug-in hybrid powertrain with dual electric motors and AWD. A 2.0L turbocharged petrol engine powers a 150 kW onboard generator, supplying electrical energy to the drive system and battery.
The range-topping Eletre X Hybrid SE produces 700 kW (938 hp), with Lotus quoting a 0–100 km/h acceleration time of 3.3 seconds. Lotus targets an electric-only range of up to 350 km from the 70 kWh battery. Together with the 52L fuel tank and onboard generator, the system provides a claimed combined range of up to 1,200 km.
Dual-valve CDC dampers and a 48V active anti-roll system help control body movement. Lotus also claims that a 350 kW DC charger can replenish the battery from 20% to 80% in approximately 9 minutes under optimal conditions.
Safety and Driver Assistance Features
The Lotus Eletre X incorporates an NVIDIA Thor processor to support its ADAS. Its sensor suite includes 30 perception sensors, 7 HD cameras, and 4D radar.
- Highway Assist: Helps maintain lane position and a selected following distance during highway driving, subject to operating conditions and driver supervision.
- Evasive Steering Support: Provides steering assistance during certain evasive maneuvers to help drivers avoid potential obstacles.
- Autonomous Parking Assist: Assists with steering, braking, and acceleration during supported parking maneuvers under driver supervision.
- Dual Digital Access Keys: Pairs an NFC tap-to-start card key with a UWB ceramic key tag for hands-free entry.
- 6.0 kW Vehicle-to-Load: Supplies external power directly from the 70 kWh battery for desert camping gear or power tools.
- Optional Intelligent Driving Pack: Adds a retractable LiDAR sensor with a dedicated washer and a physical on-off switch.
Where It Fits in the UAE Luxury SUV Market
The Lotus Eletre X enters a growing segment of electrified luxury SUVs in the UAE. Its AED 299,900 starting price is AED 70,000 below the entry-level Zeekr 9X Ultra, giving Lotus a competitive position among premium plug-in hybrid SUVs.
The 6-seat Li L9 offers a more family-oriented alternative, while the Zeekr 9X combines luxury equipment with high-performance hybrid technology. Although the Eletre X Hybrid SE reaches 100 km/h in 3.3 seconds, the higher-specification Zeekr 9X variants claim a quicker 3.1-second time and also feature 48V active suspension.
As Lotus’s official UAE distributor, AGMC oversees local sales and after-sales support.
Conclusion
With a starting price under AED 300,000, the Lotus Eletre X offers UAE buyers a more affordable alternative to the all-electric Eletre. Its plug-in hybrid architecture combines electric propulsion with an onboard petrol-powered generator, making it particularly relevant to buyers who regularly travel between emirates.
However, real-world fuel efficiency, range, and ownership costs remain important considerations. What are your views on the Lotus Eletre X and its hybrid powertrain? item.title: Ford Returns To The 24 Hours Of Le Mans With The 2027 GT41
item.text:
Ford Returns To The 24 Hours Of Le Mans With The 2027 GT41
Ford has a relatively short but lauded history with the 24 Hours of Le Mans. In the 1960s it won four years in a row with the GT40, and pop culture fell in love with the GT40 via the film "Le Mans," and then again decades later with "Ford V Ferrari." The Big Blue Oval returned to Le Mans in 2016 with the Ford GT, which came first in its class, and it continued to race through 2019. Now Ford is headed back to Le Mans in 2027 with its latest hypercar effort, the GT41. Its new FIA Endurance Championship racer was revealed Thanksgiving day on Ford Field, while a different heated rivalry plays out: the Detroit Lions vs. Chicago Bears game.
The LMDh car sports a livery featuring footballs, bald eagles, the Ford name, and the Spirit of Detroit, a statue that has sat downtown since 1958. The Ford family owns the Detroit Lions, as well as a controlling share in the auto manufacturer that bears their name. This is the kind of synergy newer oligarchs wish they could achieve.
Powering the new GT41 is a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V8 that's based on the same Coyote engine any old Ford-head can get in Mustangs and F-150s. The Coyote in the GT41 has been, of course, lovingly and painstakingly modified and rebuilt over and over again to drill down to peak Ford performance. The company then worked hard to destroy these delicately crafted pieces of machinery to ensure longevity during 24 hours of continuous driving. Ford is doing all of the development and testing in-house to make sure this new racer is the manufacturer's most ambitious program yet, born out of lessons learned during F1 Red Bull racing development.
A reserve driver
It was 60 years ago when Ford swept the race in 1966, taking positions 1, 2 and 3. The manufacturer's program ended in 1967, but the GT40 went on to three more consecutive races, just with other operators, until 1969. That car was called GT40 because it stood 40 inches from the ground to the air intake; the new GT41 has grown by a single inch.
There is a direct line from the sport of kings to the global dominance of the car, and Ford had its hand in both. It was developing and racing his own automobiles 125 years ago that got Henry Ford interested in cars in the first place. Racing awards turned into seed money for manufacturing, and the rest is history.
The Ford GT41 already has a full suite of drivers, so sorry if you were planning on putting your name into the hat. Taking the wheel will be Logan Sargeant, Tom Blomqvist, Matt Campbell, Sebastian Priaulx, Mike Rockenfeller and Nick Yelloly, plus Tom Dillmann, who was recently announced as reserve driver. Running a car for 24 hours is a lot to ask of a single driver, after all. To really cement things, Ford has a new ad campaign using Carroll Shelby's motto "Go Like Hell," with voiceover work from "Ford V Ferrari' actor Matt Damon, who portrayed Shelby in the film.
This time it's not just Ferrari that Ford is looking to beat, though Ferrari did win in 2023, 2024 and 2025, so Ford should definitely be looking over its shoulder. 2027 is proving to be a crowed year for the WEC, with 12 different factory prototypes going head-to-head at Le Mans, including this year's new kid on the block, Genesis. Next year's 24 Hours of Le Mans will be a race worth remembering, no matter who comes out on top.

item.title: Ford’s Next Le Mans Dream Is Finally Here: Meet the GT41
item.text:
- The Ford GT41 is a new Hypercar race car that the automaker hopes will help it reclaim the top spot at Le Mans.
- It’s powered by a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter version of the Coyote V-8, which, per regulations, is mated to a hybrid system.
- The car’s full reveal in its final race livery will take place before the 2027 World Endurance Championship season’s opening race in March.
You’re probably aware that all the way back in 1963, Ford tried (unsuccessfully) to buy Ferrari from old Enzo. “Il Commendatore” quite famously used the offer to secure a better deal for himself with Fiat, angering and embarrassing “The Deuce” to the point that Ford wrote a blank check to beat Ferrari at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. While Ford achieved its goal in 1966, it seems the company still holds something of a grudge. Meet the Ford GT41, the new Hypercar that Ford is hoping will put it back on the top step at Le Mans.
The GT41 gets its name because, you guessed it, the air intake at the top of the car measures 41 inches above the ground. Well, technically, the GT41 stands at 41.7 inches tall, but Ford executives told Car and Driver that they preferred the sound of GT41 over GT41.7, and they had no interest in rounding up.
The GT41’s power is naturally aspirated, of course; this is an American race team, after all, though it is mated to a hybrid system as required by regulations. Still, the combustion part of the equation is handled by a Coyote V-8 engine that has been bored to 5.4 liters and developed in-house by Ford Racing engineers.
Despite a fair amount of grandstanding about how proudly American this program is—note the American flag, eagle, football, and Statue of Liberty graphics in the livery, along with timing the reveal to take place during the Detroit Lions game on the distinctly American holiday known as Thanksgiving—Ford still won’t commit to racing the GT41 in IMSA, here in North America. The final race livery will be revealed ahead of the 2027 WEC season’s opening race in Qatar, which will take place in March.

item.title: Ford GT41 Hypercar Marks Brand's Return To The Top Class Of Le Mans
item.text:
Ford GT41 Hypercar Marks Brand's Return To The Top Class Of Le Mans
The GT41 has a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V8 built in Dearborn
Just days after Stellantis announced it would axe Peugeot's Hypercar program, Ford has given us a surprise Thanksgiving treat, officially unveiling its new GT41 Hypercar after months of testing. The car complies with the Le Mans Daytona h (LMDh) regulations, as do rivals from Cadillac, BMW, Acura, Porsche, Alpine, Lamborghini, Genesis, and McLaren. The GT41 will race alongside these cars and those made to Le Mans Hypercar (LMH) standards, like the Ferrari 499P, Aston Martin Valkyrie AMR-LMH, and Toyota GR010 Hybrid.
The GT41 is built on an Oreca chassis and, like its rivals, uses a 50-kW Bosch motor-generator and a battery pack sourced from Williams Advanced Engineering. While these parts are standardized, Ford has developed its own engine for the GT41. It's a Coyote-based naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V8 brought to life at Ford's engineering campus in Dearborn, Michigan. As with all other LMDh cars, total power from the GT41 will be restricted to 671 horsepower. An Xtrac seven-speed transmission sends power through the rear wheels.
Though Ford is unlikely to ever publicize how much grunt this new engine can deliver, videos of prototypes being tested reveal the 5.4-liter sounds just as wild as the Cadillac V-Series.R hypercar with its 5.5-liter V8.
The GT41 definitely looks the part
The Ford GT41 is certainly one of the most striking Le Mans Hypercars to look at, but unfortunately the two-tone blue camouflage finish showcased won't be carried through to the race car. The wrap includes subtle American flags, depictions of the Statue of Liberty, and a bald eagle. Though the race car won't have this same theme, the GT41 still looks very cool painted in a simpler shade of blue. The front includes a curved carbon fiber splitter and a low nose with large headlights, each fitted with three thin orange LED lights. As the GT41 is all about aerodynamics, the tops of the wheels are visible through the fenders. Speaking of the fenders, they also house the wing mirrors, and there are bold aero tunnels running behind the fenders and in front of the cabin.
Ford has also designed and developed a pronounced carbon fiber roof scoop for the hypercar that's connected to a large aerodynamic shark fin. As you'd expect, the rear includes a huge carbon fiber wing. Thin LEDs have been added to the wing's endplates, while the main taillight consists of a single curved red LED flowing across the rear. There's a pretty serious carbon fiber diffuser, too.
Ford's history at Le Mans
Ford has a long and rich history at the 24 Hours of Le Mans. A decade ago, the Ford GT won in the LMGTE Pro Class, exactly 50 years after the legendary Ford GT won the race outright in 1966 and proceeded to also win it in 1967, 1968, and 1969. Not since 1969 has Ford won the world's most famous endurance race outright, and that's what it'll be hoping to do. The GT41's name is a nod to the old GT40. Like that car, which was named because the roof was just 40 inches off the ground, the top of the GT41's roof scoop sits 41 inches above the road.
Speaking with Fox Business, Ford CEO Jim Farley appeared eager for the company to do battle with some of the most prestigious racing teams on the planet. "Now we're going back to Le Mans next summer in June to take on Ferrari and the best of the world to win Le Mans outright," he said. "It's an all-Ford effort. We're not having another company manage the athletes and the effort – this is all on Ford with some key partnerships. We're doing this because racing is an indigenous sport. Ford was basically funded from a race with Henry Ford in Lake St. Clair, and this really proves out our best technology versus these great companies."
Ford has already tested the GT41 across more than 8,885 miles during six European tests, including a 30-hour stint at MotorLand Aragón in Spain. As the car gears up for its racing debut next year, it will be tested on U.S. shores for the first time. Two cars will be entered in next year's championship, with three drivers each. These include Logan Sargeant, Matt Campbell, Mike Rockenfeller, Nick Yelloly, Tom Blomqvist, and Sebastian Priaulx. The GT41 will make its competitive debut in either March at the FIA WEC season opener in Qatar or in April at the 6 Hours of Imola.

item.text:
- Genesis is working to put the 1100-hp X Skorpio concept into production, with sales in the United States on the table.
- We knew Genesis had plans to build the concept in limited production, with sales starting within minutes of the reveal, though possible U.S. availability is a change in messaging.
- Unfortunately, thanks to its tubular frame and race engine, a production version of the X Skorpio wouldn’t be street legal.
Now that GTA VI has launched, something seems to have gotten into the minds of the executives over at Genesis. The company is actively working to bring the 1100-horsepower X Skorpio concept to production by 2030, Hyundai CEO Jose Muñoz said, according to an Automotive News report.
If you haven’t seen the X Skorpio before now, we’d forgive you for thinking it came straight out of the newest title from Rockstar Games. The batmobile-esque desert runner is built on a tubular frame with an integrated roll cage, and its bodywork is made of carbon fiber, Kevlar, and fiberglass. Oh, and it’s packing a dedicated race engine that produces 1100 horsepower, 850 pound-feet of torque, and a sound that will send all the dogs in your neighborhood scurrying for cover.
Limited production of the X Skorpio was always all but guaranteed. Genesis told Car and Driver that the first orders for the X Skorpio arrived within minutes of the concept’s reveal.
That said, Muñoz’s latest comments directly contradict the brand’s messaging when it first showed the X Skorpio concept earlier this year. When we spoke with Luc Donckerwolke, the brand’s chief creative officer, at the reveal of the X Skorpio in January, he told us outright that there were no plans to bring it to the United States and that it would instead remain a toy for wealthy customers in the Middle East. Perhaps enough American customers with the money to purchase a trophy truck as a hobby have lobbied Genesis to bring the wild machine Stateside.
Those customers will need to be willing to put up with a few drawbacks, though, because even if a production version of the X Skorpio does make its way to Genesis showrooms in the U.S., its design will keep it from earning street-legal status.

item.angle: Acura Makes Japanese-Market Debut with the U.S.-Built Integra Type S
item.text:
- The 2026 Integra Type S is now on sale in Japan, marking the first Acura-branded vehicle to reach the Japanese market.
- All Integra models are built in the United States, and the vehicles exported to Japan are identical to the ones sold stateside, right down to the left-hand-drive configuration.
- It’s unclear how many units will be sold in Japan or how much they’ll sell for, but we’d expect them to go for around $56,000.
The 2026 Acura Integra Type S is officially for sale in Japan. That might not seem like big news, considering Honda Motor Company is headquartered in Japan, but the release marks the first Acura-branded vehicle to be exported to the Japanese market. While this is Acura’s first time in Japan, it’s strangely not the Integra’s, which spent a few decades wearing a Honda badge from 1985 to 2006.
Most Acuras are designed and built in the United States and sold throughout North America. The new Integras for sale in Japan are the same as those sold stateside, meaning they’ll be left-hand-drive anomalies in a predominantly right-hand-drive market.
That also means they’ll get the same 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four that we’re quite fond of in the United States. The front-wheel-drive sport compact is only offered with a six-speed manual transmission and features a limited-slip differential, Brembo brakes, and 19-inch wheels wrapped in summer tires. The whole package comes together to reach 60 mph in a brisk 5.1 seconds.
Honda builds every Integra Type S at its assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio, and the engines come from Honda’s Anna Engine Plant, also located in Ohio. Honda began exporting vehicles from Ohio to Japan in 1988 and has shipped nearly 300,000 Hondas to Japan since then.
Honda says the Teg’s introduction in Japan marks a strong global demand for an enthusiast-centered performance sedan. If the Type S is well-received in the Japanese market, it’s likely that more Acuras could start making their way to Japan in the future. Pricing and the exact number of Integra Type S models available in Japan haven’t been released yet, but considering they’re identical to the Type S models sold on our shores, they’ll likely come in around $56,000.

item.text:
- Aptera has long promised a lightweight, solar-powered electric vehicle.
- The first customer car went to the largest investor, who plans to ship it overseas.
- They’re probably going to have to sell a few more of them to stay in business.
“Car company sells a car” seems like an unusual headline, but when it comes to Aptera Motors, things are different. For two decades, the company has been showing off concepts and prototypes, changing names and deadlines, and not actually delivering anything. That all just changed with the first delivery of a customer car.
The customer in question is Martin Hartono, an Indonesian CEO who is the largest early investor in Aptera. That investment puts him first in the queue for the production car, and he has now taken delivery. Reportedly, the car will be shipped overseas, presumably to Indonesia.
The Aptera is a three-wheeler that looks more like an aircraft than a car, capable of seating just two people. It has a 44-kWh battery pack and uses the NACS-style charger. Light weight was a target for engineers, with the stated curb weight of 2200 pounds making it more like a Mazda MX-5 than a Tesla Model 3.
The calling card for the Aptera is its set of onboard solar panels, which are said to be capable of returning as much as 40 miles of range per day. That’s 10 percent of the planned 400-mile total range and should be measurably useful in someplace sunny like California. Beyond this ability to charge on the move, the slippery aerodynamics and light weight should make it very efficient.
Hartono’s vehicle was spec’d out in a matte black finish that makes it look like something that should shoot out of a larger Batmobile. It’ll be the first of its kind on the roads once it hits them and should look especially unusual in Indonesian traffic.
A single car does not make a company profitable, so Aptera Motors still has a long way to go. However, having taken so long to arrive at this moment, perhaps it deserves a little celebration.

item.title: This Dual-Winged Mid-Engine C5 Corvette Is Real And Will Haunt Your Nightmares
item.text:
This Dual-Winged Mid-Engine C5 Corvette Is Real And Will Haunt Your Nightmares
The giant front wing was meant to solve a problem, but the mountain had other ideas.
Racing has led to a truly dizzying number of automotive innovations. Sometimes, when time is short and a racer needs to fix a problem, they come up with a wild solution. That's exactly what led to the creation of what you see here.
Built by Speedway Motors for the 1998 Pikes Peak International Hill Climb, this race car looks like a C5 Chevrolet Corvette. Corvettes are still setting records there, but that massive front wing dissolves any idea that this is somehow just a modified street car. Instead, it's a purpose-built machine that was supposed to fight for the overall victory in 1998.
Sadly, even the most ambitious ideas don't always work on a tight deadline. That was the case for driver Bobby Regester, builder Carson Smith, and the entire Speedway Motors team. The car finished third in the Unlimited division that year but was unquestionably first when it came to cars with unconventional designs.
A sprint car V8 in a Corvette suit
First, let's break down exactly what we're looking at here. According to Speedway Motors itself, the car is mid-engine and leverages a mechanically fuel-injected small-block Chevy V8, a Hewland transmission, and a custom suspension. The video description suggests the gearbox came out of a Lola IndyCar too, so this was a serious collection of parts.
It also says that it made some 800 horsepower and weighed just 1,543 pounds. That's an absolutely wild power-to-weight ratio and explains, in part, why it's perfect for the Unlimited class at Pikes Peak.
Key to that class is the ability to do just about anything you want when it comes to the car and engineering. In recent years, it's led to cars that have managed the trip to the top in well under 10 minutes. The current record set by the VW ID R, which is notably on a paved road, is under 8 minutes. Of course, that kind of speed and timing weren't remotely possible back when the Speedway Motors Corvette ran.
The wing that couldn't cure the push
In 1998, the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb still featured plenty of gravel and dirt. That put grip at a premium, and it's exactly why the Speedway team ended up adding the front wing. In testing, the team noticed that the car would understeer through most turns. That's not a lack of power but rather a lack of grip on the front tires in those conditions. To combat this, the team added the wing, hoping it would push the tires into the surface more and get the front turned in quicker.
Unfortunately, it simply didn't work. Regester ended up needing to drift the car through plenty of the turns up the mountain, and as the commentators point out in the lead video, every time he had to do that, it slowed him down and dropped him well off the pace needed to win. Ultimately, the car finished third and within about 52 seconds of Rod Millen, who won in his Toyota Tacoma with a time of 10:07.70. Nobuhiro "Monster" Tajima finished second in a Suzuki Sidekick with a time of 10:32.57.

item.title: Watch In Horror As A Ferrari 499P Slams Into A Legendary F1 Car
item.text:
Watch In Horror As A Ferrari 499P Slams Into A Legendary F1 Car
Both drivers walked away shaking hands, but the repair bills could run into the millions.
Owning a single Ferrari is a dream for many, but for some, not even a large collection of Ferrari road cars is enough. For the brand's wealthiest and most prolific collectors, the Corse Clienti program allows them to own and drive some of Maranello's most incredible cars on racetracks around the world. Corse Clienti is where you'll find Ferrari's XX models, old Formula 1 cars, and the Le Mans-based 499P Modificata. Sadly, accidents can happen on the racetrack, and that's exactly what happened during the recent Ferrari Finali Mondiali event in Barcelona.
A video shared on TikTok captured the moment things went wrong. The driver of a privately owned F2004 Formula 1 car can be seen slowing down prior to a left-hand corner when suddenly, the nose of a 499P Modificata comes into view. The Le Mans-derived prototype slams into the rear of the F1 car, briefly lifting its rear wheels off the track before it crashes back down.
Unlike road cars and most race cars, Formula 1 cars don't have brake lights, and it's possible the driver of the 499P Modificata failed to realize just how heavily the driver of the F2004 was braking for the corner. Either that or they just didn't see the bright red F1 car in front of them and couldn't jump on the brakes soon enough to avoid a collision. An incident like this makes a Bugatti Chiron crash feel like chump change.
Shortly after the crash, the two men driving the cars can be seen approaching each other and shaking hands. Were Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to come together on the track like this, we're not sure they would have been so cordial. Track officials responded to the crash and loaded the F2004 and 499P Modificata onto trucks, likely whisking them away to the pit lane to get a better look at the damage done.
This was a multi-million-dollar collision
The clip doesn't give us much of an idea of the damage suffered by the F2004, though it's fair to assume its rear diffuser will need some repairs. Additionally, expensive carbon fiber parts from the 499P can be seen flying through the air immediately after it made contact, and it too will need to be repaired before heading back out onto the track. It's unclear if vehicles in Ferrari's Corse Clienti program have some kind of specialist track insurance or not. Even if they don't, it's safe to assume the involved parties will have the funds needed to cover any repairs.
Earlier this month, a rare Ferrari 499P Modificata sold at a Swiss auction for the equivalent of $9.7 million. As for the F2004, it's the same model that Michael Schumacher raced during the 2004 F1 season. Details about the exact F2004 that was rear-ended here are unclear, so it's a little harder to estimate how much it's worth. In 2005, an F2004 sold for a then-record $3.3 million at auction, and the value of these cars has inevitably skyrocketed since then. In late 2022, a similar F2003 from Ferrari, this time driven by Schumacher himself to five race victories, changed hands for approximately $14.9 million.

item.title: Surprise! Volkswagen Brings Back The Manual Golf GTI, But Not For Long
item.text:
Surprise! Volkswagen Brings Back The Manual Golf GTI, But Not For Long
The anniversary special dusts off the third pedal and pairs it with the traditional golf ball gear knob.
To the dismay of enthusiasts, VW did the unthinkable and killed the Golf GTI’s manual a couple of years ago when it updated its long-running hot hatch. Now, Wolfsburg is thankfully bringing it back, though it won't be a permanent fixture in the lineup or a global affair. To celebrate half a century since the original Grand Touring Injection went on sale, VW is launching a three-pedal Golf GTI in Europe.
Unveiled today at the Essen Motor Show in Germany, the Golf GTI 1976 special edition takes its name from the year the Mk1 went on sale. VW will build exactly 1,976 examples, each carrying a numbered plaque inside with the inscription "ONE OF 1976." European deliveries are scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027.
But yes, the biggest news is undoubtedly the transmission. Since the facelifted Golf GTI arrived in 2024, VW has offered it exclusively with a dual-clutch automatic gearbox. The GTI 1976 changes that by bringing back a six-speed manual, making it the only stick-shift GTI in the current lineup. Not only that, but it's actually a manual-only affair.
2027 VW Golf GTI 1976
And it's not as if VW has sacrificed performance to give enthusiasts three pedals. The special edition produces 321 hp and 280 lb-ft (380 Nm) of torque. That's exactly the same output as the Golf GTI Edition 50 and 25 horsepower more than the regular Golf GTI Clubsport. Sadly, all three are forbidden fruit in the United States.
The Golf GTI 1976 isn't just a regular GTI with a do-it-yourself transmission and a commemorative badge. VW has added several styling touches to distinguish the limited-run model from its less exclusive siblings. The exterior gets an additional red GTI stripe integrated into the front splitter, along with GTI 1976 lettering.
VW has also added graphics to the roof spoiler and inside the exterior mirrors, which project the special-edition inscription onto the ground. The front and rear VW badges, as well as the rear side windows, receive a darkened finish. The car rides on 19-inch Queenstown alloy wheels with a design inspired by classic GTI models. Buyers can choose from three familiar colors: Pure White, Grenadilla Black Metallic, and Tornado Red.
2027 VW Golf GTI 1976
Inside, Volkswagen has brought back one of the original Golf GTI's most recognizable details. The manual gear lever gets a golf ball-shaped knob, just like the one fitted to the first-generation model. It's a nice touch that should appeal to anyone who appreciates the little details that made the original hot hatch so memorable.
Other changes include sport seats with exclusive GTI upholstery, red seatbelts for the outer seating positions, a red accelerator pedal, carbon-fiber decorative trim, and special door-sill plates. The multifunction steering wheel is wrapped in ArtVelours fabric.
VW hasn't stopped at cosmetic changes. The GTI 1976 comes standard with adaptive chassis control (DCC), an electronically controlled front differential lock borrowed from the Clubsport, and progressive steering. It also gets the Clubsport's Special driving profile, which optimizes the powertrain, steering, and adaptive suspension for the Nürburgring Nordschleife.
Those wanting something a little more focused can order the optional GTI Performance Package. It brings a lightweight R exhaust system with titanium tailpipes, 19-inch Warmenau forged wheels, and a comprehensively revised performance chassis.
The suspension sits 5 millimeters (0.2 inches) lower than the Clubsport's setup and 20 millimeters (0.8 inches) lower than the regular Golf's. VW has also stiffened several suspension mounting points, modified the wheel carriers to increase front-axle camber, and recalibrated the adaptive suspension and vehicle dynamics systems. Semi-slick tires are also available as an additional option for those who intend to take their special-edition GTI to the track.
2027 VW Golf GTI 1976
VW hasn't announced pricing yet, but the Golf GTI 1976 will undoubtedly command a premium over the regular model. We'd wager it will cost more than a DSG-only Clubsport, which retails for just over €50,000 (nearly $55,000) in its home market of Germany. The Edition 50 we mentioned earlier was even pricier, at €54,540. Even with what will certainly be an exorbitant price tag, getting one won't be easy given the limited production run.
It's unclear whether this is the last chance to get a three-pedal GTI. VW will move production of its hugely successful compact hatchback to Mexico in 2027, and it's reasonable to expect that to coincide with a second facelift. It would make sense, given how development of the electric Golf has been halted due to insufficient funds.
Even with a potential second refresh, we wouldn't hold our breath for the manual's return. Nevertheless, the GTI 1976 gives us hope that three-pedal hot hatches won't become extinct.
